articles.title: Sports Broadcasting under Digital Streaming Technology:  A Case Study on the Tokyo 2020 Olympics
articles.authors: Tianni Chen
articles.abstract: The Tokyo 2020 Olympics marked a pivotal moment in the history of sports broadcasting, as it became the first "Streaming Olympics" with unprecedented digital viewership growth. This paper examines the application and impact of digital streaming technology in sports broadcasting, using the Tokyo 2020 Olympics as a case study. Specifically, it analyzes the OBS Cloud, developed through collaboration between the International Olympic Committee (IOC), Olympic Broadcasting Services (OBS), and Alibaba, which enabled remote production capabilities and significantly reduced on-site infrastructure requirements. The study also explores the Content+ platform, which accelerated content delivery and provided broadcasters with near real-time access to event segments. Furthermore, it investigates how digital streaming platforms such as Peacock transformed the viewing experience by offering on-demand services, personalized content, and enhanced audience interactivity, contrasting these innovations with traditional television broadcasting limitations. Finally, the paper addresses emerging challenges, particularly piracy, and discusses the future trajectory of sports broadcasting in the context of upcoming major events like Paris 2024. The findings suggest that cloud-based streaming technology is redefining sports broadcasting standards, fostering greater efficiency, sustainability, and audience engagement, while also necessitating robust security measures to protect content integrity.

articles.title: Model Spaces in Crossnational Research: The Case of Democracy and Growth
articles.authors: Andrés Cruz; John Gerring; Carl Henrik Knutsen
articles.abstract: Knowledge cumulation is notoriously hard in crossnational research. Despite mostly sharing observational units and data sources, studies differ in myriad details that hinder comparability. Attempts to learn directly from published estimates—as in meta-analysis—must grapple with publication bias, p-hacking, disparate methodologies, and overlapping samples. We propose to construct and analyze model spaces: combinations of design choices appearing in published baseline or robustness-check models. Analyzing a literature's model space identifies the design choices that most strongly drive results, narrowing the range of potential disagreements and focusing discussions on what is most consequential. As an illustration, we present and analyze model spaces for the democracy-growth literature, showcasing the importance of (some) design choices and suggesting new research avenues.

articles.title: Evaluating methods for testing publication bias in meta-analyses with confounding covariates: A simulation study
articles.authors: Man Chen
articles.abstract: Selective publication of favorable results can bias meta-analytic estimates and threaten the validity of meta-analyses. Many methods that detect and adjust for publication bias do not perform adequately under substantial between-study heterogeneity. Heterogeneity complicates publication bias assessment because study characteristics may be associated with both effect size estimates and standard errors. These characteristics can induce an effect-precision association that regression-based diagnostics may misattribute to selective publication when such characteristics are omitted. However, it remains unclear how best to incorporate these confounding characteristics across methods and how their performance varies with confounding level, selective publication, residual heterogeneity, and the number of studies. To address this gap, I conduct an extensive Monte Carlo simulation evaluating Egger-type regression tests, residual-based tests, and a likelihood ratio test of the three-parameter selection model (3PSM) under the one-step p-value selection mechanism. Results show that when confounding covariates were ignored, Egger-type regression tests and residual analyses exhibited inflated Type I error, whereas the 3PSM likelihood ratio test maintained near-nominal, albeit slightly inflated, Type I error across conditions. When confounding covariates were incorporated, Egger-type tests had well-calibrated Type I error, residual analyses based on residualizing effect sizes alone tended to be conservative, and the 3PSM test showed slight inflation. Nevertheless, 3PSM consistently yielded higher power than other methods. Overall, the findings suggest that Egger-type regression tests and 3PSM can be used as complementary analyses for assessing selective publication when confounding covariates are present.

articles.title: An Empirical Assessment of Data Sharing and Computational Reproducibility in Sociology
articles.authors: Rio Ikeuchi; Taisuke Imai
articles.abstract: Public sharing of data and analysis code enables independent verification of published findings. While audit studies have examined data and code sharing in psychology, economics, and political science, comparable evidence for sociology remains limited. We examine 730 empirical articles published between January 2019 and June 2024 in three leading general-interest journals: American Sociological Review, American Journal of Sociology, and Social Forces. For each article, we record whether a publicly accessible replication package is available and, when materials are shared, attempt to computationally reproduce the main-text tables and figures. Overall, 9.9% of articles provide replication packages (12.2% among quantitative articles), with substantial variation across journals (5.2% to 22.9%) and research types (0% for qualitative studies, 30% for experiments). These rates fall well below those reported for political science and economics. Of the 72 packages examined in detail, more than half cannot be verified due to missing or incomplete materials. At the same time, no article is wholly non-reproducible, and 22% are fully or largely reproducible. Sociology is not unusually prone to errors when materials are shared and runnable - it simply shares them far less often. We discuss implications for journal policies and transparency standards that reflect the field's methodological diversity.

articles.title: Pediatric Cognitive Functioning Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic: Domain Specificity and School-Context Differences in a Large Multisite Sample
articles.authors: Tyler Maxwell Moore; Ruben C. Gur; Kosha Ruparel; J. Cobb Scott; Nancy Weinstein; Nancy Tsai
articles.abstract:
Background: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted children's educational and developmental environments, but its consequences have been studied mainly through academic achievement. We examined whether objective neurocognitive performance differed before, during, and after the pandemic, and whether differences were domain-, context-, and metric-specific rather than global.
Method: Participants were 33,459 children and adolescents (M age = 13.93 years, SD = 2.49; 48.4% female) assessed January 2018-December 2024 with the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery. COVID period was coded as pre-pandemic (n = 4,411), acute disruption (n = 5,208), and post-acute (n = 23,840). Age-standardized accuracy, speed, and efficiency scores across nine domains were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (children nested within families), with school type as a focal factor, and income group and sex as covariates.
Results: Period-related differences were robust but domain- and metric-specific. Verbal and spatial memory were lower during and after the pandemic, with spatial memory showing the largest effect; spatial memory speed continued to slow post-acutely. Response speed slowed across several domains, often without loss of accuracy and sometimes with improved accuracy (e.g., abstract reasoning). Attention, by contrast, was faster during and after the pandemic and more efficient afterward, with progressive improvement in efficiency and speed. The COVID Period × School Type interaction was nonsignificant, though the consistency of the dominant patterns across school types was visually uneven.
Conclusions: Pandemic-period cognitive functioning reflected changes within specific cognitive systems rather than uniform decline. Memory was most vulnerable and several effects persisted post-acutely, whereas attention and reasoning accuracy were preserved or enhanced. Separating efficiency, accuracy, and speed is essential, and speed effects warrant replication.
Keywords: neurocognition, COVID-19, pandemic, lockdown, virtual learning

articles.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
articles.authors: Robert Nosofsky; Adam F Osth
articles.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.  However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.  Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.  Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.  Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.  The model is tested using data sets from three previously reported perceptual old-new recognition studies and provides reasonably accurate predictions of performance at the level of individual items or categories, including accounts of how both false-alarm and hit rates are influenced by detailed similarity relations among items and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.

articles.title: SocialPulse: On-Device Detection of Social Interactions in Naturalistic Settings Using Smartwatch Sensing
articles.authors: Md. Sabbir Ahmed; Kaitlyn D Petz; Noah J French; Tanvi Lakhtakia; Aayushi N Sangani; Mark Rucker; Xinyu Chen; Bethany Teachman; Laura Barnes
articles.abstract:
Social interactions are fundamental to well-being, yet automatically detecting them in daily life—particularly using wearables—remains underexplored. Most existing systems are evaluated in controlled settings, focus primarily on in-person interactions, or rely on restrictive assumptions (e.g., requiring multiple speakers within fixed temporal windows), limiting generalizability to real-world use. We present an on-watch interaction detection system designed to capture diverse interactions in naturalistic settings. A core component is a foreground speech detector trained on a public dataset. Evaluated on over 100,000 labeled foreground speech and background sound instances, the detector achieves a balanced accuracy of 85.51%, outperforming prior work by 5.11%.

We evaluated the system in a real-world deployment (N=38), with over 900 hours of total smartwatch wear time. The system detected 1,691 interactions, 77.28% were confirmed via participant self-report, with durations ranging from under one minute to over one hour. Among correct detections, 81.45% were in-person, 15.7% virtual, and 1.85% hybrid. We further developed a 15-second window-level audio-only model that enables faster interaction prediction, achieving a balanced accuracy of 90.39% and a sensitivity of 91.01% on 33,698 labeled windows. These results demonstrate the feasibility of real-world interaction sensing and open the door to adaptive, context-aware systems responding to users’ dynamic social environments.

articles.title: Shared Identity and Felt Understanding in the Context of Sexual Minority Stress:  Who Gets Me, and Why?
articles.authors: Emma Laurel McGorray; Eli Finkel
articles.abstract:
Although sexual minority stress often predicts lower well-being, LGBQ+ people may be protected against these effects if they receive support that helps them feel understood. What processes are linked to greater felt understanding? Across three studies, we tested the hypothesis that LGBQ+ people feel more understood by LGBQ+ (vs. heterosexual) support providers and tested two possible explanations for this relationship: (1) LGBQ+ support providers offer higher-quality support (the support quality explanation) and (2) people’s beliefs about shared identity are linked to how they evaluate support (the interpretive filter explanation). Using varied methodologies—participants reflecting on their close relationships and evaluating both genuine and experimentally manipulated support messages—we found limited evidence for the former explanation but more robust evidence for the latter. These findings underscore the power of sharing an identity with a support provider when experiencing minority stress, while also suggesting that mere beliefs about shared identity may be a major source of that power. 
Keywords: identity, interpersonal relationships, minority stress, sexuality/sexual orientation, social support

articles.title: Reciprocal relations between peer victimization, rumination, and dysphoria: A multi-wave longitudinal study of adolescent girls
articles.authors: Pau Ortells-Faci; Riley McDanal; Yinghao Zhang; Daniel Klein; Brady Nelson; Roman Kotov; Nicholas R Eaton
articles.abstract:
Objective: Adolescence is characterized by increased vulnerability to internalizing symptoms, particularly among girls. Although peer victimization and rumination have each been implicated in this vulnerability, their dynamic, bidirectional associations with dysphoria remain poorly understood. The current study examined transactional longitudinal relations among peer victimization, rumination, and dysphoria symptoms in adolescent girls. 

Method: Participants were 550 girls (ages 13.5–15.5 years at baseline) from the Adolescent Development of Emotions and Personality Traits (ADEPT) study, assessed across five waves over three years. Self-report measures captured dysphoria, rumination, and peer victimization. A Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model was fitted to separate within-person from between-person processes and to test bidirectional associations across time, controlling for age at each wave. 

Results: At the between-person level, higher average dysphoria, rumination, and peer victimization were strongly inter-correlated. Within-person analyses showed that elevations in dysphoria predicted subsequent increases in both rumination and peer victimization, and that increases in peer victimization also predicted later elevated levels of dysphoria. Furthermore, the within-person analyses revealed rumination did not predict later changes in the other constructs. 

Conclusion: Findings suggest that, at the within-person level, changes in dysphoria and peer-victimization may be reciprocally related. In contrast, changes in rumination were only predicted by changes in dysphoria, and not peer victimization, challenging previous theory and evidence on the temporal order between the three constructs. Modeling these processes as transactional and across various levels of analyses may inform more precise estimates for multilevel prevention efforts aimed at reducing disparities experienced by adolescent girls.

articles.title: Health and Personality Contributions to Cybersickness in Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Taylor Doty; Sydney Hicks; Stephen B. Gilbert; Michael Dorneich
articles.abstract:
Background
Cybersickness reflects interactions between system (hardware and software) properties and user characteristics. Although motion sickness susceptibility is a known predictor, individual differences including transient and enduring health, psychological, and personality factors have rarely been examined and never simultaneously.

Method
Participants (N = 252) were exposed to one of five VR games. Cybersickness was assessed using self-reported symptoms (Simulator Sickness Questionnaire; SSQ) and tolerance (time in VR). Hierarchical regression models evaluated whether health, psychological functioning (affective state, psychological distress), and personality predicted outcomes after accounting for game, sex, and motion sickness susceptibility.

Results
Fatigue, pain sensitivity, and sex were key predictors of symptom severity: higher fatigue, greater pain sensitivity, and female sex were associated with higher SSQ scores. Motion sickness susceptibility and agreeableness predicted reduced tolerance. Final models explained 29.3% of variance in SSQ and 23.8% in tolerance.

Conclusion
Cybersickness reflected established stimulus and susceptibility factors as well as outcome-specific user characteristics: health-related factors and sex were associated with symptom severity; susceptibility and agreeableness were associated with tolerance.

Application
User state (e.g., fatigue), sex, motion sickness susceptibility, and tolerance-related individual differences should be considered in the design and deployment of immersive systems to improve comfort and support sustained VR use.

articles.title: Working Memory Architecture Across Verbal, Visuospatial, and Tactile Modalities: Moving Beyond Traditional Framework
articles.authors: Eyal Heled; Ohad Levi
articles.abstract: Working memory (WM) supports the temporary storage and manipulation of information, yet its underlying architecture remains debated. Prior research has examined whether WM is organized according to domain-general or domain-specific principles across processing levels (storage versus manipulation) and content domains, focusing mainly on verbal and visuospatial modalities. However, tactile WM has rarely been tested within these frameworks. The present study examined the latent structure of WM by comparing six confirmatory factor analysis models, that varied in their assumptions regarding modality specificity and processing level, thereby extending prior structural investigation to include the tactile modality. A sample of 224 young adults completed the Digit Span, Visuospatial Span, and Tactual Span tasks, each comprising forward (storage) and backward (manipulation) recall conditions. Models assuming a unitary structure, differentiated solely by processing level or modality, and mixed domain-general/domain-specific architectures, all showed poor fit. By contrast, a fully differentiated six-factor model, distinguishing storage and manipulation separately for each modality, demonstrated excellent fit. These findings indicate that WM is organized by both content and processing level, with storage and manipulation constituting a domain-specific resource, and that tactile WM forms a distinct component, which is irreducible to verbal or visuospatial frameworks. The results suggest that WM architecture is broader and more differentiated than previously proposed, highlighting the importance of incorporating tactile processing into future theoretical and empirical models of WM.

articles.title: Understanding goal selection through human limitations
articles.authors: John Branson Byers; Yael Niv
articles.abstract:
Human goal selection is simultaneously flexible and structured. Existing accounts explain this
dichotomy in terms of a biological reward function that may have proved adaptive on evolutionary
timescales. However, such explanations struggle to capture the human ability to quickly and flexibly
reevaluate goals and stimuli in response to changing contexts. In this article, we consider how
human goal selection may be shaped by cognitive limitations. We structure this perspective around
three computational-style problems that people face when selecting their own goals: consideration,
evaluation, and feasibility. Overall, we offer a brief survey of relevant literature alongside a resource-
rational account of structured goal selection without appealing to intrinsic rewards.

articles.title: Toward an Understanding of the Psychological Meaning of Physiological Synchrony
articles.authors: Chad M Danyluck; Nissa Doyle; Tyler Thorne; Andy Adler
articles.abstract: Physiological synchrony—mutual changes physiological activity between individuals—has become one of the most frequently studied yet variably-interpreted constructs in psychological science. Decades of research show that physiological synchrony is ubiquitous across relationship and social contexts, but consensus remains elusive about what it means psychologically. We advance an inferential framework for mapping observed synchrony to warranted psychological conclusions by importing classical principles of psychophysiological inference into the interpersonal domain. Building on Cacioppo and Tassinary’s (1990) logic of inference, we treat physiological synchrony as an empirical pattern whose meaning depends on three constraints: specificity (which psychological processes remain plausible given the physiological pattern and plausible alternatives), generality (the contexts, relationships, and timescales over which an interpretation should hold), and sensitivity (detectability of the theoretically relevant dynamics given measurement and modeling choices). We ground these constraints in principles of autonomic organization, emphasizing how physiological ambiguity and modes of control shape what synchrony can and cannot mean, and we use the Biopsychosocial Model of Challenge and Threat as a worked exemplar of how theory-specified multivariate profiles and motivational context strengthen inference. We further argue that model class is an inferential commitment: choices about sampling rate, observation window, preprocessing, and whether coupling is modeled as contemporaneous, lagged, or dynamical determine which forms of coordination are detectable and which interpersonal processes remain viable candidates for interpretation. By integrating contemporary synchrony approaches within this inferential framework, we provide conceptual and methodological guidance for clarifying when physiological synchrony supports strong psychological inference and for specifying the boundary conditions under which those interpretations should generalize.

articles.title: Pursuing Health in Daily Life: A Personal Projects Analysis Across Socioeconomic Position
articles.authors: Satu Koivusaari; Pam ten Broeke; Laurens van Gestel; Marieke Adriaanse
articles.abstract: Objective. Despite efforts to reduce socioeconomic health disparities, they persist worldwide. Rather than reflecting low motivation, people in low SEP value health but face other urgent demands. Yet, health behavior research often focuses on single behaviors, overlooking the daily priorities shaping health decisions. Therefore, we explored which daily goals people in varying SEP pursued, whether health was an explicit motivation underlying these goals, and how people appraised their goals. Methods and Measures. We conducted a cross-sectional online questionnaire study among participants in low (n=149), medium (n=150), and high (n=144) education. Participants listed 6-15 daily goals and rated their six most important goals on psychological appraisals derived from core motivation theories. We analyzed data using multilevel models. Results. Physical health goals were commonly pursued across SEP and participants in lower (versus high) SEP more often described health as a primary reason for pursuing their various everyday goals. Participants pursued goals of similar content and experienced them largely similarly, yet those in low SEP pursued more household-related goals and experienced their goals as less demanding. Conclusion. People in low SEP are motivated to be healthy and interventions should build on health behaviors people already pursue to fit within people's daily priorities.

articles.title: Luria’s Studies on Speech and Neuroscientific Evidence: Limbic System Functions as Biological Foundations for Socio-Cultural Psychology and Psychoanalysis
articles.authors: Maria Tereza Mendes Aversi; Tales Alexandre Aversi-Ferreira
articles.abstract: This theoretical and critical review examines Alexander Romanovich Luria’s contributions to the understanding of speech as a complex neuropsychological function and discusses their relevance as biological foundations for socio-cultural psychology and psychoanalysis. Drawing on Luria’s neuropsychological studies, classical psychoanalytic theory, and contemporary neuroscientific findings, the article analyzes speech as a functional system involving distributed cortical and subcortical networks. Particular emphasis is given to the role of the arcuate fasciculus as a key anatomical structure related to language processing and to the limbic system—especially the amygdala—in emotional modulation and unconscious processes. The analysis suggests that Luria’s conception of integrated brain functioning provides a coherent biological framework for understanding language as a mediating tool in psychological development and clinical practice. By articulating neuropsychology, socio-cultural theory, and psychoanalysis, this study reinforces the scientific basis of speech as a central mechanism in psychological assessment and intervention.

articles.title: New Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnostics and Psychological Clinical Perspectives
articles.authors: Maria Tereza Mendes Aversi; Patricia Martins Freitas; Tales Alexandre Aversi-Ferreira
articles.abstract: Recent advances in blood-based biomarkers have transformed the early diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), enabling the identification of biological risk at preclinical and presymptomatic stages in a noninvasive and accessible manner. Despite this diagnostic progress, the expansion of psychological clinical services in dementia care has not kept pace, representing a critical gap in the current management of AD. This theoretical paper critically discusses the role of psychological clinical practice in the prevention and management of AD in light of these diagnostic advances, particularly from the perspective of the International Working Group (IWG), which defines AD as a clinical-biological entity and recommends that cognitively normal individuals with positive biomarkers be considered at risk rather than diagnosed. Based on this framework and on evidence from the 2024 Lancet Commission on dementia prevention, we propose a three-phase roadmap for the integration of psychological care into multidisciplinary AD management. Phase 1 encompasses universal prevention through psychoeducation, cognitive reserve promotion, and emotional education. Phase 2 targets at-risk individuals with elevated biomarker profiles, focusing on neuropsychological evaluation, risk disclosure support, and early cognitive intervention. Phase 3 addresses individuals with established AD through cognitive rehabilitation and caregiver support. We further argue that government policies must integrate psychologists into multidisciplinary neurological and geriatric teams, and that psychology training programs must be updated to prepare professionals for preventive roles. More research on standardized psychological protocols for pre-dementia contexts is urgently needed.

articles.title: Associations of transdiagnostic and substance use disorder polygenic scores with substance use milestones in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study
articles.authors: Holly E Poore; Maia Choi; Megan Cooke; Fazil Aliev; David Harold Zald; Sarah J Brislin; Danielle Dick
articles.abstract:
Background: Genetic influences on transdiagnostic psychopathology dimensions and individual substance use disorders (SUDs) contribute to the emergence of substance use and problems. However, the relative importance of these different types of genetic influence across stages of substance use remains poorly understood. We examined associations of polygenic scores (PGS) indexing psychopathology and SUD genetic propensity with the timing of substance use milestones in adolescence. 
Methods: We calculated PGS for externalizing (PGSEXT), internalizing (PGSINT), and SUDs for participants in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study (NMax = 10,387). We used cox proportional hazards models to examine associations between PGS and substance use milestones for alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco. We ran univariable and multivariable models to estimate shared and unique contributions of each PGS. 
Results: PGSEXT was associated with endorsement of all substance use milestones (HRs = 1.13-1.66) and remained significant after accounting for the PGSINT. In univariable models, PGSINT was also associated with all milestones, though the effect sizes were smaller (HRs = 1.10 to 1.25). In multivariable models, associations of PGSINT were attenuated, but remained significant for many milestones. In contrast, with a few exceptions, individual SUD PGS were not uniquely associated with substance use milestones after jointly accounting for all other PGS. 
Conclusions: Genetic propensity for externalizing and internalizing, but not individual SUDs, were uniquely associated with substance use milestones in adolescence. These findings highlight the importance of genetic propensity for both externalizing and internalizing in understanding early substance use development in adolescence.

articles.title: A data-driven approach to the issue of ”catching up with monolinguals”
articles.authors: Cecile De Cat; Ludovica Serratrice; Arief Gusnanto; Philippe Prevost; Laurie Tuller; Sharon Unsworth
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Multilingual children in monolingual education systems are typically assessed against monolingual norms, complicating differentiation between normal multilingual development and genuine language disorders. When language experience is distributed across multiple languages, clinicians and educators struggle to determine whether multilingual learners need routine support or specialist intervention for developmental language disorders.
AIMS: This study identified: (1) the cumulative societal language (SL) exposure threshold beyond which multilingual children perform within monolingual proficiency ranges, and (2) when cumulative SL experience no longer predicts SL proficiency.
METHODS: We examined multilingual learners (ages 5–9) across three societal languages (English, French, Dutch), assessing morphosyntax via sentence repetition and receptive vocabulary (breadth and depth). Binary partition and broken stick regression identified exposure-outcome thresholds while controlling for environmental and cognitive factors. Cumulative SL exposure was measured in month-equivalents.
RESULTS: For morphosyntax, multilingual children required minimum 59 month-equivalent cumulative SL exposure to reach monolingual performance ranges. Diminishing returns occurred after approximately 57 months (4 years), beyond which morphosyntactic outcomes were no longer strongly exposure-constrained. For vocabulary breadth, no clear threshold emerged; significant differences persisted even at 94 month-equivalent exposure, with outcomes predicted more by cognitive factors and language experience richness than cumulative exposure. Vocabulary depth showed a threshold at 91 months, though sample limitations prevent firm conclusions.
CONCLUSIONS: Results demonstrate domain-specificity: morphosyntax and vocabulary show different exposure-outcome dynamics. Multilingual children require approximately 93 month-equivalent cumulative SL exposure for full morphosyntactic competence comparable to monolinguals. Before 57 months cumulative exposure, difficulties are developmentally expected; specialist referral should occur if concerns persist beyond this threshold. These findings provide research-informed guidance for contextualizing assessment expectations based on multilingual backgrounds, moving from deficit-based comparisons toward recognizing expected developmental trajectories.

articles.title: Evolving Minds: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study on Cognitive Control in Older Adults
articles.authors: Sarah De Pue; Hans Stuyck; Celine Gillebert; Eva Dierckx; Eva Van den Bussche
articles.abstract: Cognitive control is a crucial ability for daily life, especially with aging. However, the field is currently characterized by mixed findings on age-related cognitive declines, depending on the specific cognitive control subcomponent under investigation. The literature is dominated by cross-sectional designs that are biased by cohort effects and often do not distinguish between or include only one cognitive control subcomponent, typically measured by pen-and-paper neuropsychological tests. The current study used a longitudinal design in a sample of 113 older adults between 60 and 95 years old, who participated in the study yearly during a period of three years. Participants completed an extensive cognitive control test battery on each time point, focused on inhibition, updating, shifting and proactive and reactive control. Although cross-sectional age effects in updating and general age-related slowing were observed on T1, only inhibition seemed to decline over time. Longitudinal age changes were limited, possibly due to practice or retest effects which were mainly observed from the first to the second time point of the study. Further analyses into protective and risk factors and trajectories of cognitive control declines are warranted to uncover inter- and intra-individual changes in cognitive control subcomponents with aging.

articles.title: Refugee Displacement and Migration Impact Cross-Linguistic Transfer Between Arabic and English: Insights from Syrian Refugees
articles.authors: Sarah Akkad; Kaja Kinga Jasińska
articles.abstract: The role of migration experiences on first language (L1) and second language (L2) literacy and cross-linguistic transfer in refugee foreign language learners has recently received attention, but remains empirically underspecified. We investigated (1) migration-related ecological predictors of L1 reading; (2) within- and across-language predictors of reading; and (3) migration-related ecological moderators of cross-linguistic transfer from L1 phonological awareness (PA) to L2 reading. Our sample included 81 Syrian refugees between 9 and 18 years-old who resettled in Canada. Displacement in an Arabic-speaking country, shorter displacement durations, and older ages of L2 acquisition (L2 AoA) were associated with better L1 reading. Cross-linguistic transfer of phonological awareness (PA) to reading was overall greater in the L2-L1 direction, and migration experiences associated with better L1 reading were also associated with greater transfer in the L1-L2 direction. These findings highlight the need to understand refugees’ biliteracy in the context of their migration experiences.

articles.title: EPLeP: English Pseudoword Lexicon Project - A resource for investigating pseudoword processing
articles.authors: Fabio Marson; Rolando Bonandrini; Iva Saban; Simona Amenta; Marco Marelli
articles.abstract:
In recent years, psycholinguistics has seen an increase in research focused on the processing of written stimuli that are not attested in the lexicon of a given language. We introduce the English Pseudoword Lexicon Project (EPLeP), a new database of lexical decision data for English pseudowords, nonwords, and words. While large-scale behavioral data have been collected for lexical and non-lexical items in English and other languages, none of these datasets have specifically focused on pseudowords. The EPLeP database fills this gap by considering three types of English-like non-lexical stimuli: 1) morphologically simple pseudowords generated from existing English words; 2) morphologically complex pseudowords obtained by combining existing stems and existing suffixes; and 3) nonwords, not following English graphotactics. This Registered Report provides an extensive overview of the steps adopted in producing non-lexical stimuli and the criteria for their selection.
We collected data for almost 13,500 non-lexical and 4,400 lexical stimuli from 1,416 English speaking participants across four online studies. Analyses on behavioral responses show that morphologically complex pseudowords trigger the deepest level of processing, whereas nonwords elicit the shallowest processing, reflecting a crucial difference in how these stimuli affect responses to words. This database will be a valuable tool for researchers interested in both pseudoword and word processing, enabling them to evaluate hypotheses by analyzing the collected behavioral data or using them to select stimuli for future studies.
The Stage 1 protocol was accepted in principle on July 4th 2025 (https://osf.io/cz9rh/)

articles.title: Mapping psychological processes governing the sociopolitical climate system
articles.authors: Madalina Vlasceanu; Sara Madureira Constantino
articles.abstract: Climate change is often treated as a technological or environmental challenge, yet societal responses are shaped by the psychological and sociopolitical dynamics linking institutions, markets, and human behavior. Existing research has largely examined climate governance and individual psychological processes in isolation. Here we propose a multi-actor psychological systems (MAPS) model of climate action that integrates these perspectives by mapping influence pathways among seven key actors (i.e., researchers, civil society, policymakers, elites, industry, media, and the public) and identifying the processes mediating these relationships. These actors influence the sociopolitical climate system through mechanisms such as science communication, agenda setting, activism, lobbying, consumer behavior, and electoral politics. We argue that psychological processes, including risk perception, social norms, social identity, elite cueing, motivated reasoning, moral values, efficacy beliefs, and emotional processes, mediate many of these relationships and help explain why scientific knowledge does not consistently translate into policy adoption or behavioral change. By linking micro-level psychological mechanisms with macro-level institutional dynamics through the focus on these seven key actors, the MAPS framework clarifies how climate action emerges, or stalls, within complex sociopolitical systems and highlights leverage points for interventions that could accelerate climate mitigation and societal transformation.

articles.title: The Structure of Intersectional Educational Inequality Over Two Decades
articles.authors: Lisa Bardach; Mia Herkommer; Lena Keller; Nicolas Hübner
articles.abstract: Educational inequalities—systematic differences in achievement between social groups—persist worldwide. Yet long-term evidence on how such inequalities unfold at intersections of multiple social group categories (e.g., gender, socioeconomic status, immigrant background) remains limited. Using multilevel intersectional models adapted from epidemiology, we analyzed two decades of assessment data in reading, mathematics, and science (over 537,000 students from Australia, Brazil, Finland, Germany, Hong Kong, Italy, Israel, and the United States). In most countries, additive effects of gender, socioeconomic status, and immigrant background accounted for most between-group structuring in intersectional inequality. Intersection-specific components were mostly small but persistent. Large country-specific gaps separated the highest- and lowest-performing intersectional groups, with the largest gaps exceeding two standard deviation units. We highlighted intersections with pronounced (dis)advantages, underscoring the need to address compounded disparities. Overall, these findings clarify the structure of intersectional educational inequality across countries and over time.

articles.title: An R/brms tutorial on using Regularised Prediction and Poststratification for test norming
articles.authors: Taym Alsalti; Ian Hussey; Malte Elson; A Solomon Kurz; Ruben C. Arslan
articles.abstract:
Background: Sample representativeness and generalisability issues remain neglected in psychology. Test norming plays a key role because improving the representativeness of norms increases their accuracy (e.g., when using them to calculate IQ scores) and representative test norms can act as a multiplier, allowing primary researchers to obtain more generalisable inferences (e.g., about effect size) by calibrating sample statistics to the norm. Up-to-date, high-quality norms are rare in psychology.

Solution: We provide an accessible tutorial on applying Multilevel Regression and Poststratification (MRP) and extensions of it (Regularised Regression and Poststratification) using the Stan & R package brms for the purpose of deriving test norms or any descriptive estimates of population entities (e.g., prevalence of psychological disorder). 

Potential benefits: Adoption of RPP can make representative, openly shareable norms more widely available as RPP can help us derive such norms based on inexpensive online convenience samples. These norms can improve the state of (measurement) standardisation in psychology and beyond.

articles.title: Evaluating the validity of the Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA) in diagnosing ADHD: A critical examination of evidence for educational accommodations.
articles.authors: Nicole Greenwood; Hannah M Johnson
articles.abstract: The Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA) is a computerized continuous performance test frequently used for ADHD evaluations in educational environments. Given this, there is a need to examine whether the TOVA was created and tested for the purposes of academic accommodations. In addition, an integration of empirical support for validity and review of settings and populations which have been studied will help clarify important considerations if one chooses to administer the TOVA. The purposes of this review is to critically examine the validity of the TOVA for diagnosing ADHD using the unitary concept of validity, with a particular focus on the validity evidence that supports its use in educational settings. This review concludes that the TOVA’s use for academic accommodations may be useful as shown by evidence based on response processes, internal structure, and discrimination. There are concerns abouts its content, its relation to other ADHD instruments, and the populations for which the TOVA has been studied. Recommendations include considerations for administration and psychometric validation.

articles.title: Individual differences in spatial cognition: insights from a network analysis of 16 spatial skills in males and females
articles.authors: Maxim Likhanov; Yulia Kovas
articles.abstract:
Background Gender differences in almost all spatial ability (SA) facets have been robustly found across ages and cultures. The sources of these differences remain poorly understood.  
Aims The aim of the study was to examine sex differences across 16 individual measures of SA, using network analysis. 
Sample The study participants were 958 university students (35.01% males; Mage = 19.91).
Methods We used Mann-Whitney U-test to investigate sex differences in 10 small-scale (e.g., mental rotation) and 6 large-scale (e.g., navigation or orientation) SA tests. Gaussian graphical models were used to estimate networks of connections among all 16 facets for females and males separately.
Results Males performed better than females on 15 out of 16 tests. The only exception was Paper folding, for which no significant difference emerged. Gender differences for large-scale SA were somewhat greater (Effect Size (ES) from 0.10 to 0.52), compared with small-scale SA (ES from 0.09 to 0.40). Network analysis yielded almost identical SA network structures for females and males. However, there were some sex differences in centrality indices, suggesting that different SA facets serve as network hubs for males and females.
Discussion Similar network structure for males and females suggests common aeitology of spatial ability development for females and males. The observed differences in average performance and network characteristics may reflect cascading effects that involve differences in interests and activities affecting SA networks via related gene expression patterns.

articles.title: Critical review on the development and evolution of beat perception
articles.authors: Gábor Háden; Henkjan Honing
articles.abstract: Beat perception—the ability to extract a regular pulse from rhythmic sequences—is a foundational component of human musicality and a key mechanism supporting synchronization, dance, and collective music-making. Research across neuroscience, developmental psychology, and comparative cognition demonstrates that beat processing exhibits four defining characteristics: it is near-universal across human cultures, emerges spontaneously in early development, engages domain-specific predictive timing mechanisms, and appears largely species-specific. Neurophysiological evidence indicates that newborns, and even late-gestation fetuses, respond to rhythmic regularities using predictive neural processes that cannot be explained by simple interval timing or statistical learning alone. Across infancy and childhood, these early predispositions are progressively refined through auditory experience, motor development, and musical enculturation, ultimately supporting the flexible, hierarchical beat-based timing seen in adults. Comparative studies reveal that while non-human primates and other species can detect isochrony or local temporal violations, they typically fail to induce a beat, highlighting a dissociation between evolutionarily conserved timing abilities and the specialized predictive mechanisms characteristic of humans. Together, findings from phylogeny and ontogeny suggest that beat perception reflects an early-emerging, biologically prepared capacity that is further shaped by experience. Understanding its developmental and evolutionary bases offers crucial insight into the origins of human musicality and the neural architecture supporting temporal prediction.

articles.title: Beyond Nuances: Measurement Non-Invariance as a Source of Item-Level Predictive Gains
articles.authors: Kim-Laura Speck; Kristin Jankowsky; Johannes Zimmermann; Florian Scharf
articles.abstract: In personality psychology, prediction models using individual items (item-level models) often outperform models using aggregate scale scores (e.g., sum or factor scores representing facets or trait domains). This pattern is commonly attributed to stable, outcome-relevant item-specific variance ("nuances"). Using a Monte Carlo simulation, we demonstrate that violations of measurement invariance can also produce item-level predictive gains, even when no substantive item-specific effects are present in the data-generating process. We generated item responses under reflective factor models and manipulated key aspects of the measurement model (metric vs. scalar non-invariance, proportion and source of item-specific variance), the explained variance in the outcome, and sample size. Predictive performance was evaluated out of sample using regularized regression and quantified as difference in R² between item- and score-level models (∆R²). Scalar non-invariance yielded gains when the grouping variable that generated non-invariance was correlated with the outcome, whereas metric non-invariance yielded gains when the latent variable was strongly related to the outcome. These results suggest that, under certain conditions, apparent item-level predictive gains can arise from group-dependent measurement and need not reflect nuances. We discuss implications for interpreting item-level predictive gains and for evaluating predictive models across levels of the personality hierarchy.

articles.title: Theory of mind beyond beliefs: Testing attention-based social micro-processes in LLMs
articles.authors: John Muchovej; Paula Rubio-Fernandez; Julian Jara-Ettinger
articles.abstract: Vision-Language models (VLMs) can now produce fluent, socially appropriate dialogue, leading to interest in whether they have Theory of Mind (ToM). While recent work suggests that VLMs still lack coherent mental-state reasoning, this work has focused on classical propositional belief representations. Here we test a complementary, communication-relevant form of ToM: attention-based social micro-processes that support referential communication in the here and now (i.e., selecting efficient descriptions to identify a particular object for someone else). In face-to-face communication, people strategically add redundant color adjectives to facilitate the listener’s visual search, and omit them when they provide no benefit. We evaluate whether VLMs show the same strategy in a referential communication paradigm where the usefulness of redundant color words varies based on the set size and color distribution of objects. We find that VLMs can produce successful referential expressions but lack the attention-guiding strategies that make human communication so efficient. This suggests that VLMs lack the more implicit representations of attention people use in everyday communication.

articles.title: Defining brain pathways for human spoken language and vocal learning
articles.authors: Constantina Theofanopoulou; Erich Jarvis
articles.abstract: Since Paul Broca’s discoveries in the 1860s, scientist have sought to identify the brain pathways responsible for spoken language in humans. Despite extensive research, consensus on what how the spoken language pathway (SLP) is organized remains elusive. Further, studies on the neural mechanisms supporting one of the most critical components of language, vocal learning, have been limited in humas, but extensive in distantly related rare species that independently evolved the trait, particularly song-learning birds. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across multiple levels of biological analysis, including brain stimulation, inactivation, neural activity, connectivity, and gene expression, and across species, including songbirds and non-human primates, to gain a better understanding of human spoken language production and vocal learning brain pathways. Cumulative evidence suggests that the SLP can be functionally divided into two interacting subpathways: one with predominantly preparative activity before speech onset and another predominantly supporting the execution of speech. Comparisons with the vocal learning pathway of song-learning birds reveal shared organizational principles between anterior and posterior forebrain circuits across species. This synthesis provides a within and cross-species framework for future investigation of the pathways supporting spoken language production and learning.

articles.title: Asking Open-Ended Questions Promotes Personal Goal Attainment in Integrative Negotiations
articles.authors: Matteo Di Stasi; Alison Wood Brooks; Jordi Quoidbach
articles.abstract: Prior research suggests that asking more questions improves outcomes in cooperative conversations, and a vast wisdom literature espouses the power of asking questions during conflictual conversations, too: negotiation experts suggest that questions invite counterparts to disclose information and, in doing so, put askers at an informational advantage. But is this advice necessary—and is it effective? We analyzed 61,057 speech turns from transcripts of 309 dyadic integrative negotiations and used natural language processing to estimate how often people ask questions, what types of questions they ask, and how well question-asking predicts personal goal attainment (Study 1; n = 618 MBA students). Open-ended questions were rare, occurring about once every four minutes (8% of turns). Yet, asking more open-ended questions was robustly associated with personal goal attainment. Closed-ended questions and non-question statements were not reliably related to goal attainment. We then tested causality in live chat negotiations: participants who were instructed to ask open-ended questions achieved higher personal gains than those instructed to ask closed-ended questions or to only make statements (Study 2; n = 1,452 online participants), and those instructed to prepare open-ended questions before their interactions outperformed those instructed to prepare statements (Study 3; n = 372 online participants). In all studies, the benefits of open-ended questions were tied to increased information elicitation and greater value creation. Collectively, these findings offer empirical support for the widely accepted—but rarely tested—claim that negotiators (and conversationalists broadly) focus excessively on influencing (by making statements) at the expense of learning (by asking questions).

articles.title: Object recognition in autism: Within-category identification and the role of prior knowledge
articles.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Mette Elmose; Ipek Oruc
articles.abstract: Studies of visual object recognition in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are sparse and the typical sample sizes small. Here we present a series of experiments with a relatively large group of autistic participants (N = 40) examining whether they differ in performance relative to matched non-autistic participants on within-category recognition of animate objects, moving objects and natural objects. We also examined whether the autistic group would show reduced performance on the recognition of novel objects. Evidence supporting this latter hypothesis would suggest that potential differences are perceptual in nature rather than reflecting differences between groups in prior knowledge and/or interest. Across comparisons the evidence was found to be 3 – 8 times more likely under the hypothesis of autistic participants not performing less efficiently than non-autistic participants. These findings were stable across a range of prior-widths, suggesting that the results are robust. We discuss the results in relation to previous reports of differences and lack hereof and argue that as of yet no studies have demonstrated altered object recognition ability in autism that cannot be explained by lexico-semantic dysfunction or a more intermediate visual problem (i.e., configural processing).

articles.title: Exploring the Role of Physical Effort in the Rewarding Value of Sedentary Behavior
articles.authors: Silvio Maltagliati; Pam ten Broeke; Philippe Sarrazin; Ryan Rhodes; Erik Bijleveld; Genevieve Fridlund Dunton; Cedrick Bonnet; Benjamin Gardner; David A. Raichlen; Matthew W Miller
articles.abstract: Objective: Sedentary behavior is commonly studied based on the value of the higher-order task being performed, such as watching TV, using a phone, or playing video games. However, it is possible that the low physical effort associated with these behaviors also contributes to their appeal. That is, individuals may be drawn not just to the task but to the low effort it is paired with. This study aims to test this possibility by manipulating body position (sitting vs. standing) while participants engage in a familiar sedentary task (i.e., playing Tetris). Methods: To test this hypothesis, we manipulated body position during a smartphone video game task to examine how sitting versus standing affected the rewarding value assigned to the game. Results: Our results (two independent studies, N = 228 and N = 129) show that the rewarding value of this sedentary behavior also stems from the low effort cost associated with sitting. Conclusions: These findings underscore the critical role of effort perception in shaping sedentary preferences and provide valuable insights for interventions aimed at reducing excessive sedentary behavior and promoting more active lifestyles, such as targeted strategies to increase the valuation of physical effort.

articles.title: Group-level behavioral effects are not enough: applying the GRIPS framework to a spontaneous magnitude preference task in house crickets
articles.authors: Bartosz Baran; Krzysztof Cipora; Julia Klimecka; Mateusz Hohol
articles.abstract: Group-level analyses dominate behavioral research, but averaging across individuals and repeated measurements can obscure whether an effect is robust, prevalent across individuals, and stable within them over time. We propose the GRIPS framework, a four-level analytical approach that decomposes behavioral effects into [G]roup-level effects, [R]obustness across within-organism subsets of the data, [I]ndividual [P]revalence, and Intra-individual [S]tability. We illustrate the framework using a spontaneous magnitude preference task in house crickets (Acheta domesticus), tested across seven consecutive daily sessions in an open-field arena with two vertical black bars differing in width. At the group level, crickets spent more time near, and made more visits to, the thinner bar, whereas first choice remained at chance. At the robustness level, within-individual resampling showed that the visit-based effect was significant in most session subsets, the time-based effect was directionally consistent but limited in robustness, and first choice showed no consistent effect. At the individual-prevalence level, the proportion of crickets showing the group-consistent direction was significantly above chance for visits, but not for time spent near the stimuli or for first choice. At the stability level, preference measures showed negligible within-individual stability across days, whereas two locomotor descriptors, Emax and sinuosity, showed moderate repeatability and served as internal benchmarks indicating that the design could detect stable behavioral components. Overall, the findings show that robust group-level outcomes can be poor proxies for individual-level tendencies, motivating routine reporting of the full GRIPS decomposition rather than reliance on aggregate summaries alone.

articles.title: Object recognition in autism: Shape configuration and Category-specificity
articles.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Ipek Oruc; Mette Elmose
articles.abstract: Face recognition in autism is well-researched and up to 1/3 of autistic individuals are reported to have severe face recognition difficulties. In comparison, there are few reports on object recognition performance in autism, and the findings are rather inconsistent. Here we report results from a series of object recognition tasks performed by autistic (N = 41) and matched non-autistic participants. Across tasks we varied the demand placed on perceptual differentiation, the structural similarity of the objects, and the salience and value of global shape information (the object’s bounding contour) relative to local shape information (details) in the recognition process. Our main hypothesis was that when local shape information was less salient than global shape information, and when both types of information needed to be integrated to support performance, autistic participants would perform less efficiently than non-autistic participants. This hypothesis was not fulfilled as the autistic group performed just as efficiently as the non-autistic group across all tasks. We discuss our findings in the context of previous reports of object recognition performance in autism and argue that former reports of impairments might reflect lexico-semantic rather than perceptual processes.

articles.title: Modelling structured trial-by-trial variability in evidence accumulation
articles.authors: Steven Miletic; Niek Stevenson; Luke Joseph Gough Strickland; Andrew Heathcote
articles.abstract: This tutorial presents a comprehensive framework for modelling structured trial- by-trial variability in evidence accumulation models (EAMs). Traditional EAMs assume independent and identically distributed (IID) parameters across tri- als, which fails to capture the temporal dynamics and structured variability inherent in cognitive processes. We introduce Bayesian hierarchical methods to estimate EAMs that incorporate trial-level variability, offering both data- driven and theory-driven approaches. Data-driven methods describe how decision processes vary across trials using trend models, while theory-driven methods explain adaptations in response to specific factors. By moving beyond the IID assumption, our approach allows for a more precise characterisation of dynamic cognitive processes such as learning, adaptation, and fatigue. This tutorial pro- vides step-by-step guidance on implementing these methods using the EMC2 package, demonstrating their application to experimental paradigms involving choice and response time data.

articles.title: Uncertainty in Psychology Research Articles: The Evolution of Its Frequency Between 2005 and 2020
articles.authors: Rrita Bajraktari; Olivier Klein; Arnaud Destrebecqz; Bertin
articles.abstract: This study examines the expression of uncertainty in psychology research articles published between 2005 and 2020. Uncertainty has an important role in scientific articles since it enables researchers to position themselves regarding claims and facts they present. It shapes both the interpretation of findings and their long-term impact. In the introduction, we present the common operationalization containing uncertainty found in the literature under different names: Epistemic Modality, Hedging and Uncertainty, along with their overlaps. Building on this conceptual framework, we operationalized uncertainty through a list of uncertainty cues. In the second instance, we proceeded with our preregistered plan to analyze 15,021 peer-reviewed articles between 2005 and 2020 across four subdisciplines in Psychology: Social, Clinical, Cognitive-Neuropsychology, and General psychology. We measured uncertainty via the UC1000 metric (frequency of uncertainty cues per 1,000 words). We expected that the replicability crisis, also coined confidence crisis, would result in an increase in uncertainty cues across this period. Contrary to our first hypothesis, the results revealed a small decline in uncertainty cues over time. We propose two explanations within the broader context of the replicability crisis, weighing competing interpretations: increased clarity in reporting or unsupported bold claims? Disciplinary differences were pronounced and stable over time: Social Psychology consistently showed the highest uncertainty levels, while Cognitive-Neuropsychology remained the lowest. Although discipline-specific norms were known, our results further suggest that such norms persist even within subdisciplines. Given the growing concerns in recent years regarding the quality of research articles, our theoretical and empirical contributions aim to foster evidence-based discussions on the role of uncertainty in scientific communication.

articles.title: The Sensation Modulating Network: Haltability as the architectural ground for object-directed phenomenology
articles.authors: Nagarjuna Gadiraju; DurgaPrasad Karnam
articles.abstract: We propose the Sensation Modulating Network (SMN): the cognitive agent conceived as the whole body, organized at every anatomical scale by opponent dynamics, built from Sensation Modulators — tissue that senses and acts through one substrate — paired into Coordinated Action Zones routed by a body-wide broadcast. It is an inclusive model of the body: one in which physical variables such as gravity, material properties such as elasticity, and the topological and geometrical structure of the body itself do constructive cognitive work. This paper is scoped to what such a body constructs at its foundation — a self-model, a world-model in that self's frame, and object-directedness — each constructed by the body's physics, not assumed as a primitive. We present the architecture as a generative model: one small kit of primitives whose morphological variations (chain, sheet, tube, layered, appendicular) construct experience by the same mechanism, an invariance we demonstrate for the self-model across body plans and scales. The central thesis is that haltability — the active holding of an opponent equilibrium — is the architectural condition object-directed phenomenology requires; a second principle, that an object is a bundle of more than one property, carries the construction from a felt resistance to a genuine object. A companion computational bench realizes each construction as a runnable, falsifiable experiment, each with a pre-registered order parameter and matched foil. We close by placing the principal competing accounts — sensorimotor enactivism, active inference, ecological and affordance-based theories, and others — as limiting cases within a wider landscape, stating in each case the falsifiable criterion that would tell them apart, and by giving systems and cognitive neuroscience its place: the nervous system as the integrating core that makes the body one, not a commander over it. On this account, the cognitivism–4E impasse stems from an incomplete account of the embodied agent's architecture: its resolution begins not with the brain alone but with the whole body, modelled this way.

articles.title: Are autistic individuals better at finding targets in complex figures (disembedding) than non-autistic individuals and does it reflect a local processing bias?
articles.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Mette Elmose
articles.abstract: It has been suggested that individuals diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) perform better than non-autistic individuals in tasks requiring the finding of simple shapes embedded in more complex figures/backgrounds. This advantage has been suggested to reflect a perceptual bias in autism with processing of details (local information) being weighted more than information regarding the context in which the details are part (global information). However, the empirical evidence is mixed regarding this local advantage – probably due to the use of small samples (median N = 15) – and direct evidence for a correlation between disembedding performance and local processing bias is lacking. Examining both issues in a relatively large sample of autistic individuals (N = 40), and by means of sensitive and reliable measures, we find more support for the null hypothesis than for the alternative hypotheses regarding a disembedding advantage in autism and superior disembedding performance being related to an increased local information processing bias.

articles.title: Debunking decreases mistaken causal inferences: A direct replication of Irving et al. (2022)
articles.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Keyi Zhang; James Edward Bartlett
articles.abstract: We conducted a direct replication of Irving et al. (2022) examining whether a debunking statement reduces mistaken causal inferences from correlational evidence. We randomly allocated participants to read a news article containing either a correction statement (n = 65) or a no-correction control (n = 64). Participants in the correction group made fewer causal inferences (delta = 0.65, 95% HDI [0.30, 1.00]) and more correlational inferences (delta = 0.72, 95% HDI [0.36, 1.07]) compared to the no correction group. In exploratory analyses, we also supported the robustness of their findings to alternative modelling choices. Our findings represent a successful direct replication of Irving et al.

articles.title: Traditional plant-based dishes: A gateway to sustainable eating
articles.authors: Marija Branković; Anastasija Budžak
articles.abstract: In traditional societies, reducing meat intake can feel threatening to traditional identities, particularly ethnic and/or religious ones. Despite this, a large part of traditional cuisine is plant-based, and fasting is observed as a valued religious tradition. We therefore sought to investigate preferences for a selection of traditional plant-based dishes. We expected them to be evaluated more positively when labeled as Lenten than when they are labeled vegan, as Lenten is a familiar and relatively positively perceived label in the local context. In a preregistered between-subjects experiment (N = 273), we attached the label to the product description, which also included a verbal description and a product photo, for ten traditional plant-based dishes. Results indicated that the mean preference score in the vegan and Lenten conditions did not differ significantly. Our findings suggest a strong overall preference for traditional plant-based dishes, regardless of how they are labeled (i.e., as vegan or Lenten).  The preference for traditional plant-based dishes was positively correlated with less meat consumption, more experience with plant-based products, as well as non-reflexive religiosity and the observance of fasting. The findings thus show no negative effects of the vegan label, and the profile of correlates suggests that these dishes can appeal to both traditionally and non-traditionally inclined individuals. We discuss the traditional plant-based dishes as a nutritional “gateway” between tradition and modern plant-based diets. These implications are encouraging and potentially applicable to promoting plant-based diets.

articles.title: Social Determinants of Depression in a Small-Scale Subsistence Population
articles.authors: Tanay Katiyar; Paul L. Hooper; Eric Schniter; Bret Beheim; Daniel Cummings; Charlotte Debras; Daniel Eid; Hillard Kaplan; Ben Trumble; Jonathan Stieglitz
articles.abstract:
Background: In industrialised societies, it is well-documented that mental health has social determinants. Yet, these factors remain understudied in small-scale subsistence populations.

Methodology: We quantified variation in depression sum-scores among T simane forager-farmers (n = 2665) at the level of households (n = 1098) and communities (n = 68), after adjusting for
individual-level factors. Subsequently, we investigated whether specific features of these social levels — distance to market town, community size, and household size — explained observed variation in sum-scores.

Results: Depression sum-scores showed modest household (ICC ~ 0.07) and community (ICC ~ 0.07) variation. While there was moderate evidence of weak associations between lower depression
sum-scores and larger community & household sizes, this did not explain higher-level variation. However, follow-up item-level analyses revealed that these results differed between depressive
symptoms. For instance, feeling useless (ICC ~ 11%) and mistrust (ICC ~ 10%) exhibited more community-level variation than other symptoms while increased market town distance associated with
decreased rumination, but increased mistrust.

Conclusions and Implications: Our results suggest that depressive symptoms may vary at social-organizational levels, though the specific determinants remain unknown. Some symptoms have
higher sensitivity to socio-ecological factors, which can be obscured by sum-score analyses.

articles.title: Integrating active inference with evolutionary systems biology: a framework for reconstructing music and language evolution
articles.authors: Felix Haiduk; Tudor Popescu
articles.abstract: Humans possess two elaborate, culturally transmitted communication systems: music and language. In cognitive science, the evolution of these capacities has been studied through two main approaches: identifying and analysing either features conserved across cultures or traits conserved across species. Both approaches leave key questions unanswered: which ancestral stages corresponded to which features, in what order traits evolved, and whether and how music and language diverged from a common precursor system. We propose adapting an evolutionary systems biology (ESB) framework, originally intended to identify causal interactions in evolving systems and specify their possible evolutionary trajectories. This approach provides mechanistic explanations for phenotypic development and evolutionary transitions. In transferring it to evolutionary cognition, we link recent insights into neurodevelopment and niche construction to processes of active inference, processes mediating between cognitive traits and spectrotemporal features present in the niche. We consider the free-energy landscape over belief states as the cognitive analogue of the ESB epigenotype. We reason that social interaction creates conditions so that cognitive traits and niche-structuring features can mutually shape each other over developmental and evolutionary timescales. For music and language evolution, we argue that these processes can be quantified using our framework, and that recently developed computational models provide the infrastructure for evolutionary simulations to this end. Our evolutionary cognitive systems biology framework thus offers a novel approach to analysing the biocultural evolution of music and language.

articles.title: Unsupervised Statisticians Ignoring Orders: An Investigation into Methodological Assumptions for Biological Psychiatry with UK Biobank Data
articles.authors: Owen Matthew Truscott Thomas; Guro Pauck Bernhardsen; valeria vitelli; Soili Lehto
articles.abstract: Ordinal data are widespread in psychiatric research, especially in the form of Likert scales, but can be challenging to adequately model due to their ordered and discrete nature. In this work, we investigate the role of model specification for ordinal data in large-scale psychometric applications, focussing on the methodology of model-based clustering. Methods deliberately designed for ordinal data (ordinal likelihood) demonstrate the undesirable behaviours of instability and computational expense in large-scale data sets, while in comparison other more generic methods (e.g., Gaussian or multinomial likelihoods) offer preferable scalability and usability in the applications considered. In two “big data”-scale UK biobank data sets, using the PHQ-9 and a CIDI-SF-derived symptoms of depression, we examine the robustness of model-based clustering to likelihood choice (Gaussian vs Multinomial vs Ordinal). We further pursue an extensive, systematic simulation approach to understand the data properties driving the computational behaviour. Our results simultaneously uncover clinically relevant depression subtypes, and  illuminate the pragmatic decision-making landscape spanning theoretical well-specification and practical convenience in two real-world large-scale applications and extensive simulations. The findings further highlight the demand for more robust and scalable tools designed for unsupervised learning of large-scale ordinal data.

articles.title: Early predictors and adolescent outcomes of a multi-informant model of general (p-factor) and informant-specific child psychopathology
articles.authors: Megan Frith; Christopher B Stride; Richard Rowe
articles.abstract:
Background
Models of general psychopathology (p) are typically based on single informant data, risking the conflation of p, and its associations with risk factors and outcomes, with common method variance. We previously proposed a multi-informant trifactor model of adolescent psychopathology comprising multi-informant p, informant-specific and specific psychopathology factors. Here we test whether this structure generalises to middle childhood; whether early childhood antecedents predict the components of our emergent model and whether its components predict age 17 outcomes, reported independently from the informants who defined the model. 
Method
Participants were 13,596 seven-year-olds from the Millennium Cohort Study. Confirmatory factor analyses compared seven multi-informant psychopathology structures based on parent- and teacher-reported Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire data. Structural equation models linked the components of the best fitting model to parent-reported risk factors at age five and adolescent-reported psychosocial outcomes at age 17. 
Results
A trifactor model of psychopathology fit better than alternative structural models, with loadings invariant across informants. Prospective predictors of age seven p included parental psychological distress, lower household income and bully victimisation. Age seven p predicted psychological distress, suicide attempts, non-suicidal self-injury, and low educational attainment at age 17. Parent- and teacher-specific factors showed loading patterns similar to our previous work and predicted a number of adolescent-reported outcomes. 
Conclusion
The multi-informant trifactor model that we identified during adolescence generalises to psychopathology at age 7. Our evidence of early risk factors for p may help to identify children at risk for broad psychopathology. Outcomes were self-reported by adolescents a decade after the age 7 trifactor model was formed from parent and teacher reports, so common method variance cannot explain these associations. Informant-specific variance appears prognostically informative and therefore seems to represent more than a methods artefact.

articles.title: Longitudinal Links Between Executive Function and School Wellbeing During Transition to School: A Two-Wave Study in England and Hong Kong
articles.authors: Siu Ching Wong; Chengyi Xu; Caoimhe Dempsey; Jean Heng; Laura Katus; Elian Fink; Claire Hughes
articles.abstract:
Starting formal schooling is a major milestone that brings multiple challenges for children’s
wellbeing and is also characterized by rapid growth in executive function (EF; Cadima et al.,
2015; Thompson & Steinbeis, 2020). To examine dynamic links between school wellbeing
and EF, we adopted a longitudinal multi-informant cross-cultural design. Overall, 361 children
(England: n = 206, Time 1 Mage = 5.39 years, SD= 0.31, 80% White British; Hong Kong:
n = 155, Time 1 Mage = 5.02 years, SD= 0.33, 99% Han Chinese) and their caregivers (89%
mothers in England and 88% mothers in Hong Kong) were seen twice, with one-year interval
between time points. At each time point, children completed three EF tasks. Children and
parents rated child school wellbeing. For both sites, EF increased over time, but parent-rated
school wellbeing declined; in England, child-rated school wellbeing also declined over time.
Latent change score models showed that, in both sites and for both informants, the association
between EF and school wellbeing was non-significant at school entry, but positive at Time 2.
This shift likely reflects increasing regulatory demands as schooling becomes more formal in
nature. Baseline EF did not predict change in school wellbeing in either site, and baseline
school wellbeing did not predict change in EF, with one exception: in Hong Kong, parent-
rated school wellbeing at Time 1 predicted gains in EF. These multi-informant, cross-cultural
findings underscore the need to support both child EF and school wellbeing as distinct, co-
developing domains during this critical period.

articles.title: Change blindness in pigeons (Columba livia) and humans (Homo sapiens):  A comparative study using landscape photographs
articles.authors: Kiwako Shimada; Miki Yoshida; Kanna Okamoto; Arii Watanabe; Tomokazu Ushitani
articles.abstract: Change blindness is a visual attentional phenomenon in which changes between two scenes are difficult to detect when a brief visual disruption is inserted between them.
