Fifty-nine healthy participants learned aversive object-scene pairs followed by a fear acquisition phase. After 24 hours, participants underwent extinction whilst practising retrieval stopping. We hypothesised greater reductions in unconditioned stimulus (US) expectancy for objects following retrieval stopping (No-Think) than standard extinction (View) over time. The results showed that US expectancy decreased during extinction, though retrieval stopping was not superior to standard extinction.  Bayesian analysis provided weak evidence that intentional retrieval stopping is not a superior alternative to standard extinction. Further research should investigate the long-term effects of retrieval stopping on fear recovery and generalisation.

articles.title: Longitudinal Attendance Trajectories Across Three Academic Years in English Secondary Schools: Predictors and links with Internalising Symptoms
articles.authors: Christopher Knowles; Qiqi Cheng; Emma Thornton; Neil Humphrey
articles.abstract: Objective:  To identify longitudinal attendance trajectories across secondary education, examine their eco-systemic predictors, and assess associations with emotional difficulties.  Method: Linked #BeeWell survey and administrative data were analysed for 28,736 pupils aged 12–13 at baseline across 156 secondary schools in Greater Manchester. Piecewise latent growth mixture modelling identified attendance trajectories across nine consecutive school terms (Autumn, Spring and Summer terms 2021/22–2023/24). Multinomial logistic regression examined predictors across individual, family, school, peer, and community domains. Emotional difficulties were modelled as a latent growth process to compare class-specific intercepts and slopes.  Results: Three attendance trajectories were identified: Consistently High (92.4%), Progressive Decline (5.1%), and Decline & Recover (2.5%). Socioeconomic disadvantage was most strongly associated with sub-optimal attendance trajectories (ORs = 2.94–4.97), with dose–response effects for neighbourhood deprivation. Special educational needs were also associated with increased risk, while protective factors included good physical health, sufficient sleep, school belonging, and minoritised ethnic group membership. LGBTQ+ identity was not independently associated in fully adjusted models. Pupils following sub-optimal trajectories reported higher emotional difficulties at baseline (d ≈ .34–.41), but no differences in rates of change over time were observed.  Conclusion: Attendance trajectories are socially patterned and linked to pre-existing vulnerabilities. Emotional difficulties appear to precede, rather than result from, divergence in attendance. Findings support multi-tiered interventions combining universal strategies to promote school belonging with targeted support addressing socioeconomic disadvantage and mental health needs. Evidence of a recovery trajectory highlights the potential for timely intervention during secondary education.

articles.title: Feeling academia: An in-depth analysis of researchers’ achievement emotions
articles.authors: Lara Abel; Luisa Ciampi; Mollie Etheridge; Allison Beggs; Yingjie Li; Molly Smih; Noam Tal-Perry; ARRC - Debbie Birkett; Marie Collier; Katherine M. Dawson
articles.abstract: This study uses a combination of qualitative research methods for an in-depth examination of Early Career Researchers’ (ECRs) and Principal Investigators’ (PIs) achievement emotions and emotion management strategies at a research-intensive UK university. As part of an online survey, 15 ECRs and eight PIs submitted reflective letters providing rich insights into their professional lives. We interviewed five participants to deepen our understanding of their experiences. Our qualitative analysis combined thematic and affective coding, drawing on appraisal theories of emotion. We found that positive emotions were reported in relation to aspects inherent to the academic professions, both in relation to teaching and research, including supporting others and fulfilment in research. Negative emotions related to structural conditions including precarity, low pay and lack of institutional support. Participants highlighted the importance of social and personal resources for coping with the negative emotions associated with these structural issues. Through the process of letter writing, participants actively regulated their emotions using reappraisal and self-reassurance mechanisms. We discuss how narrative research methods, such as the letter methodology, can be used as powerful action research tools for studying and intervening on academic emotions and propose workshop formats as levers for improving academics’ professional experiences.

articles.title: Hierarchical neural adaptation supports flexible speech perception across rates
articles.authors: Jérémy Giroud; Lucy Jane MacGregor; Máté Aller; Saskia Helbling; Helen Blank; Manuel Mercier; Agnès Trébuchon; Benjamin Morillon; Matthew H. Davis
articles.abstract: Human listeners effortlessly understand speech which they hear at a wide range of speaking rates. Yet the neural mechanisms that support the flexibility of successful speech processing remain unclear. Recent evidence suggests time-locked neural responses to features of connected speech (e.g. the amplitude envelope) in auditory brain regions, yet key questions about whether and how these brain mechanisms encode speech at different rates remain. Fixed accounts suggest rate-invariant neural encoding mechanisms, whereas adaptive accounts predict rate-adaptive neural encoding in which speech processing adjusts to changes in speech rate. To adjudicate between these hypotheses, we measured neural responses to speech (podcasts, and sentences) presented at three different rates while neural activity was measured using magnetoencephalography (MEG) or stereoelectroencephalography (sEEG). For both recording modalities we observe hierarchical organisation of neural encoding of the speech envelope across the cortex within the left hemisphere: early auditory regions encode speech in a largely rate-invariant manner, whereas higher-order temporal and frontal lobe regions display rate-adaptive encoding, reflected in both changes to the temporal structure of neural responses and in the ability of neural encoding models to generalize across different speech rate conditions. Together, these findings reveal a general computational principle whereby flexible speech perception across temporal scales is supported by a hierarchical transformation from early rate-invariant to later rate-adaptive neural processes.

articles.title: The development of forward models for efficient exploration
articles.authors: Danaja Rutar; Matthew Sims
articles.abstract: Developmental learning proceeds through exploration, yet its sensory consequences are not initially organised as usable evidence. The challenge is to explain how learners acquire the architecture that makes sensory change interpretable and organises experience into structured states over which predictions can be composed. We propose that development progressively constructs predictive and compositional forward models, through which prediction structures experience and the resulting structure expands predictive scope. We identify four stages and, for each, specify the limitation it addresses and the resulting gain in exploratory efficiency: progressive construction of recurring sensory and sensorimotor structure from approximately 7.5 to 24 weeks’ gestational age (GA); emergence of proto-somatic forward models around 24 weeks GA; emergence of proto-environmental forwards model around 34 weeks GA; and compositional chaining of predictions around eight months postnatally. By reorganising the learner’s effective data, each stage makes the next capacity learnable, casting development as a self-scaffolding process.

articles.title: Designing Vocabulary Multiple-Choice Tests For Exploring Word Frequency Effects In Distributional Semantics
articles.authors: Joseph Patrick Levy; John Bullinaria
articles.abstract: The representation of word meanings by positions in a vector space is now widely used across a range of psychological models and technological applications. There exist many different approaches for creating such vectors, with Distributional Semantic Vectors (DSVs) often produced directly or indirectly from word co-occurrence statistics derived from large corpora of natural language. One of the most widely used methods for testing and comparing their performance is the Vocabulary Multiple-Choice Question (VMCQ) test in which the best synonym of each tested word has to be identified from among a set of distractor words. By manipulating the details of the questions, they can also be used to explore finer-grained aspects of performance, in particular the effect of word frequency. Many such tests have already been created for testing human linguistic ability, and they are easily applied to DSVs by basing the choice on simple vector distances. This paper demonstrates that, while the general VMCQ approach is useful for testing DSVs, designing VMCQs specifically for DSVs provides better results than using existing tests created for humans. To do that, an improved VMCQ scoring method is first developed that provides considerably more statistically reliable results, and that allows a series of new evaluation methods to be introduced that enable improved explorations of the effect of word frequency on DSVs and VMCQs. These eventually lead to the identification of an improved general VMCQ approach for exploring frequency effects in DSVs, which is tested successfully on a representative set of nine previously published DSVs.

articles.title: Effects of Auditory and Motor Cues on Syntactic Planning during Sentence Production in Free- and Fixed-Word-Order Languages: Evidence from Hindi and English
articles.authors: Swati kushwaha; Niharika Singh
articles.abstract:
Previous studies have shown that visual attention influences syntactic planning during sentence production. The present study examined whether this influence can extend to auditory and motor modalities and how it further interacts with the language type (fixed vs free-word order) and its status as L1 and L2. For this Hindi-English bilinguals completed a picture description task in Hindi (Experiment 1) and in English (Experiment 2) in which cue modality (auditory vs. motor), cue type (agent cued vs. patient cued, referent position (patient-left vs. agent left) was manipulated. For English, the effect of L2 proficiency was also added as factor. For both languages, utterance type, speech onset latencies and first fixations on patient referent was analyzed.
The result showed that auditory cue led to more object-initial sentences than motor cue condition in Hindi, whereas no influence of modality was found on the passive constructions in English. However, patient cueing led to increased production of passive constructions in low L2 proficiency speakers, indicating that low proficiency L2 speakers relied more on the external attention cueing for sentence planning. Speech onset latencies were found to be longer for motor cue condition than auditory cue condition in both the languages, suggesting higher processing demands for motor cueing. Referent position exerted a robust effect on syntactic choices in both the languages, such that speakers produced more object-initial construction in Hindi and passive voice construction in English when the patient was position to the left than when it was positioned right in the display. Eye movement data further revealed that combined influence of referent position and cue modality in early allocation of attention. Together the findings of the present study suggest that influence of attention on syntactic planning extends beyond visual attention and are shaped by language specific grammatical properties, spatial attention and language proficiency.

articles.title: Stimulus Certainty Modulates Similarity-Induced Memory Bias and Swaps
articles.authors: Nursima Ünver; Keisuke Fukuda; Rosanne L. Rademaker
articles.abstract: People tend to bias their report of a target item briefly held in visual working memory (VWM) towards novel visual input shown during the delay, especially when the novel non-target input is deemed similar to the target item. We investigate whether the magnitude of this influence, known as the similarity-induced memory bias (SIMB), depends on the certainty with which the target and non-target items are encoded. Across two experiments, participants (N = 64) remembered the direction of a dot motion stimulus (target) for later report. On 80% of trials, a second dot motion stimulus (non-target) appeared during the delay, and participants judged whether its motion direction was similar or dissimilar to that of the target. In Experiment 1, stimulus certainty was manipulated by changing the motion coherence of the target and non-target in tandem. Here, low target and non-target coherence resulted in reduced recall precision, less confidence in memory report, and amplified SIMB. When the target and non-target coherences were manipulated independently (Experiment 2), reduced recall precision and increased SIMB magnitude were most evident when target coherence was low. Furthermore, modeling revealed that the SIMB reflected two dissociable memory errors, namely bias of the memory target toward the non-target, and replacement of the target by the non-target. While both contributed to SIMB in most of the conditions, replacement errors happened more frequently under low target coherence. Overall, these findings suggest that a non-target item can interact with a memory target, evoking two types of memory error that are shaped by stimulus certainty.

articles.title: When Can Associations Be Interpreted as Evidence for Psychological Theory? Closing the Theory-to-Model Gap in Observational Research
articles.authors: Peter Hilpert
articles.abstract:
Observational studies in psychology routinely report regression coefficients as associations, thereby avoiding unwarranted causal claims. This leaves a deeper inferential question unanswered: under what conditions can an estimated association legitimately be interpreted as evidence for a psychological theory?
  Statistical inference alone cannot answer this question. It establishes what can be concluded about the parameter defined by a specified statistical representation, but not whether that parameter represents the theoretical relationship under investigation. This additional inferential step requires the underlying theory to determine its intended statistical representation, a condition we refer to as the theory-to-model gap.
  An illustrative example demonstrates why this matters. The same dataset and theoretical relationship yield regression coefficients ranging from a strong positive association (B = 0.81) to virtually none (B = 0.05) to a negative association (B = −0.07), depending solely on the statistical representation that is estimated. Each estimate is statistically valid within its own model, yet at most one can represent the intended theoretical relationship. Simply relabeling a coefficient as an association does not resolve this ambiguity.
  We introduce theory specification as the scientific process through which theories determine their intended statistical representations and propose a preliminary framework for evaluating when this condition is met. Rather than judging whether a theory is correct, the framework provides an operational criterion for determining when a statistical parameter may legitimately be interpreted as evidence for a psychological theory. By extending a central inferential principle from modern causal inference beyond causal interpretation, the framework provides a foundation for more rigorous theory development and more transparent statistical modelling in observational psychological research.

articles.title: Age-related shifts in metacognition are driven by converging confidence for correct and error judgments across the lifespan
articles.authors: Lenard Dome; Madeleine Moses-Payne; Vasilisa Skvortsova; Tobias U. Hauser
articles.abstract: Introspective accuracy shapes self-determined decisions, yet how it changes across the lifespan is unresolved. The evidence at the extremes of adolescence and old age points in conflicting directions. In a unique lifespan dataset N=6,000 spanning 10-90 years, we traced age-related effects of perceptual metacognition. Using piecewise regression, we found that metacognitive sensitivity, tracking how well confidence distinguishes between correct and erroneous decisions, followed a biphasic trajectory with a peak in adolescence and a steady decline towards older age. Critically, we found two distinct drivers for this biphasic trajectory: whilst confidence in correct decisions increased early in life, plateauing after adolescence, confidence in erroneous responses continued to rise throughout life, driving the metacognitive decline later in life. This means that metacognition  is stratified rather than unitary, where correct and error confidence operates with distinct lifespan profiles, a critical insight when considering how to support impoverished metacognition at either end of the lifespan.

articles.title: Dimensions of Experiencing a Turrell Skyspace in Relation to Well-being
articles.authors: Eleftheria Pistolas; Stephanie Louise Miller; Isaac Lim Wei En; Ryan Joseph Slaby; Alexandra Victoria Alvarez; Johan Wagemans; Matthew Pelowski
articles.abstract: Despite a growing body of research connecting many art activities to mental well-being or mental and physical health, empirical evidence regarding the actual, lived experience of artworks and how this might relate at a mechanistic level to specific outcomes, remains limited. This is especially so for contemporary art, which is often thought to not be particularly appreciated among the public, thus raising serious questions when applying public resources to its creation or installation, as well as when considering public access, or when trying to connect these artforms to specific societal benefits. The present study considers these gaps with one notable contemporary example––James Turrell's Skyspace series. Unlike many contemporary examples, these are often sought-after among the general public, specifically because of the presumed positive results they might elicit. They have thus been a recipient of many public resources and initiatives and have also been anecdotally, but not empirically, connected to both contemplative but also transformative engagements.  Using a within-participants crossover design, participants (N = 143) experienced a Skyspace and completed pre- and post-experience questionnaires assessing well-being, embodied cognition, and identifying experience type via latent profile analysis. This was contrasted (with counterbalanced order for all participants) with engagement with nature (contemplation of a garden), which itself provides an emerging target for public funding and arts comparison. While descriptive trends suggested higher aesthetic ratings for the Garden, statistical models revealed no main effects of space on liking, beauty, or interest, but several time effects. In contrast, the Skyspace elicited higher mood arousal and increased reports of feeling emotions or activation in the "head," consistent with more introspective, cognitive engagement. Latent profile analysis identified more Harmonious experiences in the Garden and more Transformative experiences in the Skyspace, associated with cognitive challenge and insight. Both spaces enhanced positive affect. However, the Experience Type was a stronger predictor of both aesthetic evaluation and well-being outcomes than the space itself, with Novel and Harmonious experiences associated with the most positive outcomes across both spaces. These findings convey the interplay between space, person, and context on aesthetic and affective experiences.

articles.title: A Mixed-Methods Study Exploring the Impact of Minority Stress on Trauma and Dissociation Symptoms Among Sexual and Gender Minorities: Preliminary Evidence for an Adapted Four-Dimensional Model of the Traumatized Self
articles.authors: Mina Pichtikova; Sandhya Narikuzhy; Ally H. Villeneuve; James Mirabelli; Jakub Wolf; Paul Frewen; Ruth Lanius; Taylor Hatchard; Hygge Schielke; Emily Levitt
articles.abstract:
Background: Sexual and gender minorities (SGMs) face a higher risk of mental health disorders due to stigma associated with their identities. Research demonstrates that minority stress (e.g., discrimination, microaggressions, and internalized stigma) negatively affects mental health outcomes among SGMs, including trauma-related symptoms. However, no studies have explicitly examined the relationship between minority stress, trauma-related symptoms, and dissociation using a mixed-methods approach.
Methods: Forty SGM participants with diverse intersecting identities participated in the study. Using a convergent parallel mixed-methods design, we conducted semi-structured qualitative interviews to examine experiences with minority stressors and administered clinical assessments and quantitative measures of minority stress, trauma symptoms, and dissociation. Qualitative themes pertaining to trauma-related symptoms were extracted and converged with scores from our quantitative minority stress measure, allowing us to investigate differential thematic presentations based on minority stress severity. A mediation analysis examined whether dissociation may be a trauma-related response to minority stress.
Results: Our study revealed four qualitative themes pertaining to minority stress-based trauma symptoms among SGMs: hypervigilance, negative sense-of-self, emotion dysregulation, and dissociation. These themes differentially presented depending on minority stress severity. Quantitative analyses revealed that trauma symptoms mediate the relationship between minority stress and dissociation symptoms, suggesting that dissociation may be a trauma-related response to minority stress.
Conclusions: This study is among the first to employ a mixed-methods approach to examine the relationship between minority stress, trauma symptoms, and dissociation among SGMs. Findings suggest that dissociation may represent a trauma-related response to minority stress and provide support for adapting existing frameworks, such as the 4-Dimensional Model of the Traumatized Self, to better understand trauma-related mental health disparities associated with minority stress. Collectively, these findings provide a foundation for developing interventions aimed at addressing the psychological consequences of minority stress among SGMs.

articles.title: Assessing Fairness in AI-Assisted Writing Scoring: Two Indices for Quantifying the Magnitude of Group Differences
articles.authors: Guanyu Chen; Sirui Wu; Chiyu Zhang; Amery D. Wu
articles.abstract: Fairness evaluation in automated essay scoring (AES) requires more than determining whether group differences exist. It also requires evidence about how large those differences are, which group they favor, and whether they warrant further attention. This study introduces two model-level indices, Conditional Mean Disparity (CMD) and Conditional Odds Disparity (COD), for evaluating group differences in predicted writing scores after accounting for human-rated proficiency. CMD quantifies disparity on the predicted score scale, whereas COD quantifies disparity using the relative odds of receiving higher predicted scores. The indices were demonstrated using writing samples from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus and four AES systems representing traditional statistical modeling, deep learning, and prompt-based large language model scoring. The findings showed that CMD and COD provided interpretable estimates of disparity magnitude across systems and captured information that was not reflected in scoring performance alone. By emphasizing the size and direction of observed group differences, the proposed indices can support fairness evaluation, model comparison, and decisions about whether further examination is needed.

articles.title: A shared EEG signal for the maintenance of visually and linguistically evoked objects: theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling
articles.authors: Wesley Leong; Gerry Altmann
articles.abstract: How do our brains represent events in language? Recent work has shown that when we comprehend state-change events, multiple representations corresponding to different states of an object are simultaneously activated. As the sentence unfolds and the object is cued for retrieval, areas of the brain associated with representational conflict become more activated in proportion to how dissimilar the object-states are to each other. Before being retrieved, however, these object-states have to be actively maintained in the brain. What are the neural mechanisms by which we do so? Across two EEG experiments, we present evidence that, during sentence processing, the maintenance of multiple object-states in state-change events is supported by a neural signal that has been frequently linked to visual working memory: left temporal theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling.

articles.title: A Permutation-Based Network Invariance Test Using the Network Similarity Metric
articles.authors: Simran Johal; Natalie Bondurant; Esther Ulitzsch; Mijke Rhemtulla
articles.abstract:
One research question of interest in psychometric network analysis is whether two
populations—clinical versus non-clinical, patients before versus after treatment, or subgroups
differentiable by region or demographic characteristics—have the same cross-sectional network
structures. However, most network comparison techniques, such as the widely-used Network
Comparison Test (NCT), only assess whether two groups’ network structures are statistically
different, and not to what degree. Ulitzsch and colleagues (2023) proposed a network similarity
metric, sF , that quantifies the level of similarity between two networks, but recommend that it be
interpreted only after a separate test of network invariance indicates differences between the two
networks.

We propose a network invariance test, NCT-sF , that allows researchers to simultaneously
test for invariance while also interpreting sF . NCT-sF uses the permutation approach of the NCT,
but with sF as its test statistic. Through a Monte Carlo simulation study, we evaluate the
performance of this method in terms of Type 1 error and power, and compare it to the NCT for
invariance. Results suggest that NCT-sF has appropriate control of the Type 1 error rate, and that
power to detect differences is increased when sample size and/or the differences between
networks are large. Furthermore, it is often equally as powerful as the NCT for testing network
invariance, especially when moderate changes are spread throughout the entire network. NCT-sF
provides a way for researchers to compare cross-sectional networks and interpret the degree of
similarity between them.

articles.title: An Updated State-Level Collectivism-Individualism Index in the United States
articles.authors: Mark S. Chen; Simon M. Li; Bee Lee; Bronwen Lathrop; David Park
articles.abstract: Collectivism-individualism shapes cognition, emotion, and behavior, yet within-country differences in the U.S. remain understudied and often rely on a collectivism index developed over 25 years ago. In this study, we report an updated Collectivism Index to assess variation across states. Building on prior frameworks, we integrated diverse behavioral and demographic indicators, including family structure, marriage stability, religiosity, transportation practices, and self-employment. While overall patterns broadly aligned with historical findings, notable shifts emerged, suggesting sociocultural changes over the past two decades reshaped the relative expression of collectivism across states. Consistent with prior work, collectivism was higher in southern than northern states and showed little association with longitude. However, the latitudinal gradient was significantly weaker than that observed in the original index, suggesting potential cultural assimilation across latitudes. Additionally, higher collectivism scores were associated with lower rates of marijuana use, binge drinking, and depression, and with greater cultural tightness, consistent with country-level findings in extant literature. These findings underscore the persistence, evolution, and psychological correlates of cultural patterns within the U.S. and provide a contemporary spatial tool for examining how regional cultural differences relate to psychological outcomes.

articles.title: Identifying Latent Mechanisms Underlying Uncertain Risk-Taking: Methodological Insights from Risk Contingency Reversal in the Balloon Analogue Risk Task
articles.authors: Zachary Aaron Tefertiller; Thorsten Pachur; Franziska Knolle
articles.abstract:
Introduction:
Research using the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART) has primarily interpreted behavior in terms of individual differences in risk preferences. However, because participants must learn the probability of a balloon exploding from experience, BART performance also depends on learning processes that are rarely distinguished from risk preference. We examined latent learning mechanisms across different risk levels and following a reversal of risk contingencies, dissociating belief updating from subjective valuation of potential gains or losses.

Methods:
In an online sample of healthy adults (n=118, 63 female), we implemented an adaptation of the BART with three different risk levels and subsequently reversed the learned color-risk associations. We compared three hierarchical models to identify the latent mechanisms that best described participant behavior. We then investigated whether schizotypy and psychotic-like experiences were associated with behavioral or modelling parameters.

Results:
Adjusted pumps neither differed between reversal phases nor were associated with subclinical traits. The Exponential Weight Mean Variance (EWMV) best explained behavior. Individuals updated risk-level beliefs faster post-reversal, while faster pre-reversal updating was associated with heightened delusional ideation and schizotypy. Choice stochasticity was highest after and negative schizotypy was associated with greater stochasticity overall.

Discussion:
Manipulating and reversing risk levels in the BART revealed adaptive learning processes not captured by adjusted pumps. Although adjusted pumps showed no differences, computational modelling revealed differences in belief updating and behavioral stochasticity. Associations with subclinical measures were modest and require further investigation.

articles.title: Short-term Evaluation of a Voice-Based Generative AI Emotional Support Companion: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.authors: Nicolas Röver; Lukas Wolf; Valerie Forman-Hoffman; Patricia Areán; Bennet Feld
articles.abstract: Elevated anxiety symptoms are common, yet many people lack adequate support because professional care is costly, scarce and stigmatised. AI-based systems may help overcome these barriers by providing scalable, on-demand support. In this study we evaluated Sonia, a voice-based generative AI companion teaching techniques from cognitive behavioural therapy. Four hundred US adults with elevated anxiety symptoms were randomly assigned 1:1 to Sonia or passive web-based psychoeducation based on World Health Organi

articles.title: Who Relies More on Context?Individual Differences in Word Predictability Effects Across Reading Proficiency and Language Background
articles.authors: Erez Milsthen; Yaakov Raz; Victor Kuperman; Noam Siegelman
articles.abstract:
Word predictability is a central determinant of eye movements during reading, with
multiple theories aiming to explain how reading proficiency and one’s background as a
first (L1) vs. second (L2) language reader relate to individual differences in
predictability effects. However, findings from individual-differences studies and L1/L2
comparisons have been mixed, with interpretation complicated by limited reliability,
varied methods for estimating predictability, and difficulty separating L1/L2 status from
proficiency. Here, we leverage large-scale data from the Multilingual Eye-movement
Corpus (N = 1201) to revisit these questions. We estimated readers’ predictability
effects using Bayesian hierarchical models, with word predictability quantified using
both human cloze and language-model surprisal. We then examined the reliability of
resulting estimates and their relation to reading proficiency and L1/L2 status. After
establishing which measures are reliable, we show that stronger predictability effects
correlate with lower proficiency indexed by slower reading rate, with stronger
correlations among L1 than L2 readers. We also find that once controlling for
proficiency, L1 readers show larger predictability effects than L2 readers. These
findings suggest that predictability effects reflect multiple sources of variance, including
the overlap between objective and subjective predictability, and one’s reliance on
contextual support given their knowledge of the writing system.

articles.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families. The magnitude of the association varied meaningfully across SES indicators and motivational components, but only marginally across academic domains. Educational home resources (e.g., books, educational materials) showed stronger associations with achievement motivation than parental education or occupational status, and self-efficacy exhibited the largest association among motivational components. The association increased over historical time but declined following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After controlling for academic achievement, the meta-analytic average association between family SES and achievement motivation remained statistically significant, but its magnitude was attenuated. These nuanced findings highlight the complex association between family SES and students’ achievement motivation, emphasizing the multidimensionality of both constructs and providing an important empirical foundation for evaluating, refining, and advancing psychological theories that address the link between family SES and students’ achievement motivation.

articles.title: Are items from current self-report measures adequate for assessing autistic traits in women? Insights from a modified Delphi study with autistic women and professional experts.
articles.authors: Nora Uglik-Marucha; Jude Fredman; Tala Al-Shurafa; Clarissa Ragrag; Francesca Happé; Hannah Belcher; Silia Vitoratou
articles.abstract:
Sex/gender-related measurement bias in autism measures has been proposed as a factor contributing to the underdiagnosis of autistic women, yet research in this area remains limited. This study builds on the small but growing body of work addressing this gap by using a modified Delphi methodology to reach consensus among autistic women and academics/clinicians on the most relevant items from five measures of autistic traits: Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-50), Broad Autism Phenotype Questionnaire (BAPQ), Comprehensive Autistic Trait Inventory (CATI), Girls Questionnaire for Autism Spectrum Condition (GQ-ASC), and Ritvo Autism and Asperger Diagnostic Scale-14 (RAADS-14), and to evaluate each measure’s suitability for autistic women in their current form.

Thirty-three autistic women and thirty-three academics/clinicians participated in the study. Each participant was asked to rate the relevance of individual items to the experiences of autistic women and to indicate whether each measure comprehensively captured experiences relevant to this group. Agreement on relevance was calculated separately for each group using the item-level content validity index (I-CVI) and the modified kappa statistic (k*), with scale-level content validity indices (S-CVI/Ave) derived for each measure.

The findings showed broad consistency in relevance evaluations between the two groups. The RAADS-14 was rated as the most relevant measure for assessing autistic traits in women, followed by the CATI, while the remaining questionnaires were associated with lower perceived relevance. However, none fully captured experiences relevant to autistic women, indicating construct underrepresentation that warrants further investigation. Items assessing masking were identified as valuable for inclusion to enhance the relevance of autism measures for women. In contrast, items related to attention to detail and imagination appeared less useful for assessing autism more broadly or for capturing subtler presentations of autistic traits, or may not be suitably phrased for autistic women. The most relevant items identified across the five measures can be considered valid across clinical, academic, and lived-experience contexts, providing a foundation for refining existing scales to better capture the experiences of individuals with subtler presentations of autistic traits.

articles.title: Social desirability bias obscures mind-wandering reports
articles.authors: Shivang Shelat; Alexis Raquel Clubb; Barry Giesbrecht; Jonathan Schooler
articles.abstract: The study of mind-wandering relies on the assumption that people accurately introspect and report on their attentional state. Yet self-reports may be distorted by extraneous motives, such as a desire to appear attentive. Across two sustained attention tasks, we demonstrate that social desirability bias is systematically linked with task-unrelated thought (TUT). In Experiment 1, higher social desirability bias scores predicted fewer subjective TUT reports during a reaction time task, despite no relationship with objective response times (RTs). This suggests a self-presentation effect rather than true attentional differences. Time pressure during thought probes further weakened RT–TUT coupling. In Experiment 2, controlling for social desirability bias enhanced the ability of an objective, RT-based real-time triggering procedure to predict deeper subjective TUT reports in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). The alignment between objective triggers and subjective reports was strong for low-bias individuals, but weakened for those high in bias. Triggers were also less effective at capturing working memory lapses in participants prone to deliberate mind-wandering, suggesting that intentional off-task thinking manifests differently in behavior. The results show that social desirability bias can obscure TUT reports and should be considered in a science of attention and thought.

articles.title: Low Resilience or Low Sample Mean? Misattribution and Misapplication of Brief Resilience Scale Cutpoints
articles.authors: Bryan Queme
articles.abstract: The Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) is among the most widely used measures of psychological resilience. Researchers increasingly categorize respondents as low, normal, or high resilience using fixed cutpoints (<3.00 / 3.00–4.30 / >4.30). Yet the origin of these cutpoints is rarely traced: they have spread through the literature largely detached from their source and their authors' intended use. We reviewed 32 studies that categorized BRS scores, extracting the cutpoints used, the sources cited for them, category proportions, and sample means. For four studies reporting proportions without means, we calculated and validated an inverse normal estimation method to recover sample means (r = .992, mean absolute error = 0.10). Of 32 studies, 25 (78%) applied the fixed cutpoints, and 17 of those 25 (68%) attributed them to Smith et al. (2008), the original BRS validation paper, which contains no cutpoints. The actual source is Smith et al. (2013), a paywalled book chapter with 29 times fewer citations. Among fixed-cutpoint studies, low-resilience prevalence was almost perfectly predicted by the sample mean (r = −.988); the lower a sample's mean, the more respondents fell below the fixed threshold. In contrast, studies that derived cutpoints from their own mean and standard deviation, as Smith et al. (2013) intended, classified a stable 17–21% as low regardless of the mean. Smith et al. (2023) have since published updated norms based on 121 studies that shift the boundaries to <2.67 and ≥4.00; no reviewed study used them. Fixed cutpoints make low-resilience prevalence a function of the sample mean instead of resilience. We recommend a dual approach: updated norms for absolute comparison, and sample-derived cutpoints for identifying low resilience within each sample.

articles.title: Recommendations for Recruiting Clinically-Relevant Stratified Samples Across Race/Ethnicity, Gender, and Socioeconomic Status Using the Prolific Online Platform
articles.authors: Julia Machina; Kimberly A. Muellers; Xiqiao Chen; E. Samuel Winer
articles.abstract: Though online sampling methods have progressed, psychology literature continues to include primarily white, educated, upper-class samples. This work will outline the methodology of a stratified community study examining demographic differences in fear of happiness and depression among U.S. adults. Drawing on prior research suggesting variation in emotional processes across social identities, we implemented a fully crossed stratified sampling design to ensure equal representation across race/ethnicity (Black, Asian, Latine, White), gender (cisgender male, cisgender female), and socioeconomic status (SES). Eligible participants were 18-65 years old and residing in the U.S. SES categories were defined as ≤ $50,000 (low), $50,000 - $100,000 (middle), and ≥ $100,000 (high). A priori power analysis (G*Power) indicated a target of 42 participants per cell (N=1,008) to detect medium effects. Following the exclusion of 75 uncategorizable cases, the per-cell target was adjusted to 38, maintaining adequate power for medium-to-large effects. Participants were recruited in SES-based blocks via Prolific. Procedures to preserve stratification, confidentiality, and analytic rigor will be discussed, highlighting methodological considerations for equity-focused psychological research. These methods can ensure adequate power and representation when examining relationships between intersectional identities and psychological phenomena in online samples.

articles.title: Loops All the Way Up: Recurrency as an Implementation-first Primitive for Consciousness
articles.authors: Zefan Zheng; Robert Chis-Ciure; Peter Thestrup Waade; Anna Eiserbeck; Jaan Aru; Thomas Andrillon; Bechir Jarraya; Lucia Melloni; Georg Northoff; Fernando Rosas
articles.abstract: Consciousness science is fragmented, and empirical investigations are confined within each theory of consciousness’ (TOC) framework. Proliferating ToCs accumulate anomalies without progress, operating orthogonally. The principle of recurrency – functional and architectural – offers a unifying, mechanistic scaffold for consciousness to arise. We show that all theories tacitly invoke feedback loops and can be re-expressed along a single axis of recursion. Four nested levels, viz., cellular, local inter-areal, global, and lateral, map onto state, phenomenal content, manipulative access, and experiential similarity, respectively, thus tying evolved anatomy to phenomenon. The traditional phenomenal-versus-access stand-off dissolves into a graded cascade wherein deeper recursion expands the set of reportable, behaviour-driving variables. Recurrence is favoured evolutionarily, and ontologically, rebutting feed-forward, “unfolding” objections, while brain-body loops ground selfhood, and complete action loops with the environment. Furthermore, clinically, targeting recurrent pathways promise new biomarkers, and alleviation, in disorders of consciousness (DoCs). The field urgently requires this conceptual unification that is biologically plausible, mechanistic, and empirically testable.

articles.title: Executive Functioning as a Developmental Scaffold for Emotion Regulation: Longitudinal Neural and Behavioral Associations Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Kayleigh Esparza; Shannon O'Conner; Ava J. White; Dalia El-Shafie; Jacob Armstrong; Martin P Paulus; Robin Aupperle
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a critical developmental period marked by rapid changes in limbic and prefrontal regions, alongside gains in executive functioning and the development of emotion regulation strategies. Prior work suggests reciprocal relationships between executive function and emotion regulation, with each being important for supporting optimal developmental outcomes. However, further understanding the longitudinal relationships and underlying neural mechanisms is important for informing the timing and targets of intervention approaches. The present study utilized longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (N = 11,868) to examine these relationships from approximately ages 9–16. Exploratory factor analyses were conducted using fMRI data from the emotional N-back task, identifying three factors each for the 2-vs.-0-back and Faces-vs.-Places contrasts, corresponding to Sensorimotor-Insular, Central Executive, and Visual-Occipital networks. Cross-lagged panel models were used to test prospective associations amongst these network factors, scores on the emotion regulation questionnaire, and an NIH Toolbox executive function factor score across time. Results indicated that the Central Executive factor of the 2-vs.-0-back contrast predicted subsequent executive functioning across all time points, with some evidence of bidirectional associations in preadolescence. Moreover, executive functioning at ages 13–14 positively predicted both cognitive reappraisal and emotion suppression at ages 14–15, while neither emotion regulation strategy predicted later executive functioning. These findings highlight the dynamic and reciprocal nature of neural and behavioral development across adolescence and support the importance of executive network development for supporting cognitive function, and for executive functioning as an important developmental scaffold for emotion regulation strategy use.

articles.title: Is conscious perception necessary to direct attention? A replication of Jiang et al. (2006): Stage 2 Registered Report
articles.authors: Yung-Jung Chen; Ryan Bradley Scott; Zoltan Dienes
articles.abstract: The relationship between attention and consciousness has been debated for decades. Observing attentional biases induced by visual stimuli below the conscious threshold is one way of providing evidence for the independence of attention and conscious perception. Among such studies, Jiang et al. (2006) found a strong priming effect below the objective conscious threshold with high sensitivity, in showing attentional biases to nude images suppressed by continuous flash suppression (CFS). In our replication, we found moderate Bayesian evidence for the unconscious attraction from opposite sex nude images below the subjective conscious threshold in heterosexual participants. This supports the theory that attention and consciousness are dissociable, and the idea that sexually attractive visual stimuli capture attention even when rendered unconscious. The results have been checked for computational reproducibility by an independent statistician, full report at https://osf.io/dr35v/files/te58h.

articles.title: Sex differences in behavioral and neural mechanisms of active avoidance in rodents
articles.authors: Shannon Ruble; Maria M. Diehl
articles.abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent neuropsychiatric disorder worldwide, and women are approximately twice as likely as men to be diagnosed with an anxiety disorder over their lifetime. Maladaptive avoidance is a defining feature of this disorder; therefore, considering how sex as a biological variable impacts these processes is critical. This review focuses on preclinical rodent studies of active avoidance and aims to uncover whether there are any sex differences in the behavioral expression of active avoidance and the neural substrates that guide this behavior. We provide an overview of behavioral processes that have been reported in the two-way shuttle, lever-press, and platform-mediated avoidance tasks, followed by the neural mechanisms within the amygdala, prefrontal cortex, and other regions recruited in these tasks. These findings have implications for ethological and clinical relevance in understanding how the behavioral and neural processes of active avoidance go awry in anxiety and other neuropsychiatric disorders.

articles.title: What is the Worst Gift to Bring to a Wedding? Measuring Humor with Quirky Questions
articles.authors: Paul Joseph Silvia; Vi Bui
articles.abstract: Humor production—the intentional generation of funny ideas—is an interesting instance of creative thought, but methods for studying humor are relatively underdeveloped compared to other areas of creative cognition. The present research develops and evaluates the quirky questions task, a text-only creative humor production task that was designed to be intuitive for participants and suitable for the field’s growing interest in automated response coding and item generation. A sample of adults (n = 320) completed six quirky question prompts (e.g., What is an unusual thing to bring to a classroom show-and-tell?) along with measures of personality and other individual differences. Their responses were judged for funniness by five human raters. Latent variable models showed that funniness was associated with higher openness to experience, spending more time creating the responses, and writing longer responses, all findings that replicate past work with other creative humor production tasks. Demographic differences were minor at most. Overall, this task appears to be a promising addition to the humor assessment toolbox.

articles.title: Verbal ability in trials of cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety and depression in youth: A systematic review of selection criteria, measurement and treatment outcomes.
articles.authors: Isabella Metcalfe; Courtenay Norbury; Duru Kaya; Georgina Krebs; Sarah Louise Griffiths
articles.abstract: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is a verbally mediated first-line treatment for anxiety and depression in young people. Developmental language disorders are common in this population, yet the impact of verbal ability on CBT response or drop-out remains unclear. This systematic review considered randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of CBT or CBT-based interventions in youth with anxiety or depressive disorders. Eligible studies reported anxiety, depression, or treatment adherence/drop-out as an outcome and include a measure of verbal ability or language-based selection criteria. We searched EMBASE, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and CINAHL on 9th January 2025 and 4th January 2026. Sixty-eight studies were eligible. No studies recruited participants with developmental language disorders, and sixty-five studies excluded participants with poor verbal ability. Ten studies reported taking measures of verbal ability, while only one primary RCT and six secondary analyses examined the relationship between verbal ability and outcomes. Findings were mixed, and overall evidence quality was variable. Trials of standard CBT for anxiety and depression in youth systematically exclude individuals with poor verbal ability using subjective criteria, while rarely reporting participants' verbal ability. Consequently, evidence on whether verbal ability influences CBT outcomes is lacking. Further research is needed to determine the effectiveness of CBT for language disorders.

articles.title: The Stress Test: A Mechanistic Simulation of Response Bias and Item Fragility in Psychological Scales
articles.authors: Jose Ventura-Leon
articles.abstract: Validating a scale requires spending a sample before knowing whether its structure will withstand response biases. This work presents a pre-empirical stress test that turns item wording into the parameters of a response-process simulator: a language model rates the desirability of each statement, embeddings detect near-paraphrased pairs, and the intended structure is subjected to increasing doses of six classical biases up to the breaking point, along with the items that fall first. On synthetic scales no alarms were fabricated (median clean structure = 1.00), and the seeded desirability halo was detected with a sensitivity of 0.97 and a specificity of 1.00, whereas two paraphrased pairs sank the probability from 0.90 to 0.01. The estimated desirability was stable across language models and correlated between 0.42 and 0.86 with the observed endorsement. Applied to nine public scales, the forecast separated those with real structural problems from the rest, and desirability was the only bias whose breaking point discriminated among scales. An additional calibration study with four Spanish couple scales showed that the real local dependences escaped both the lexical trigger and a paraphrase judge, and that half of them responded to positional adjacency, which grounds the scenario-based design of the engine. An optimistic forecast indicates the absence of wording-induced risk, not a warrant of good fit or of theoretical validity. Its use as an audit prior to fieldwork, together with its limits, is discussed.

articles.title: Word Order Processing in Dyslexic adults: Evidence from grammaticality decision tasks
articles.authors: Mahmoud Medhat Elsherif; Kevin Paterson
articles.abstract: Reading relies on the seamless integration of rapid, automatic word recognition and the structural constraints of word order. Non-dyslexic readers exhibit a transposed word effect (TWE), evidenced by lower accuracy and slower reaction times for stimuli containing word transpositions derived from grammatical, rather than ungrammatical, base sentences. The TWE suggests a reliance on top-down syntactic constraints rather than purely flexible processing. The nature of these constraints in dyslexic adults, however, remains poorly understood. The present study investigated whether dyslexic adults possess the same positional flexibility as non-dyslexic readers, or if their processing is constrained by serial-order impairments. We used parallel, central serial, and progressive displays across three experiments with 372 adults (62 participants per group). Across all display types, we observed a TWE in accuracy and a three-way interaction between group, condition, and display type. Specifically, while non-dyslexic readers showed a larger TWE in the parallel display compared to the central and progressive displays, dyslexic readers exhibited a larger TWE in the central and progressive displays compared to the parallel display. These findings indicate that the TWE is a marker of high cognitive cost linked to noisy, temporally processed orthographic input during sentence-level interpretation.

articles.title: The Joint Effects of Measurement Error and Model Misspecification on Statistical Interactions
articles.authors: Aljoscha Rimpler; Henk Kiers; Don van Ravenzwaaij
articles.abstract: Measurement error in predictors and unmodelled interaction effects pose recurring challenges in psychological research, yet their joint consequences for regression analysis have not been analytically characterized. We show that classical measurement error and the omission of a true interaction effect are not independent sources of bias, but become entangled such that their combined effects cannot be recovered by applying standard corrections for either problem alone. Specifically, we derive closed-form expressions for the probability limits of OLS regression weights under joint measurement error and interaction omission, characterize the implied asymptotic residual structure, and establish expressions for model fit and prediction error for infinite samples. A key finding is that the residual contributions from measurement error and interaction omission can partially cancel each other out, so that prediction error reduces marginally while leaving coefficient bias large. As a consequence, qualitatively different models can become difficult to distinguish by standard fit metrics, even in large samples. Furthermore, we demonstrate via Monte Carlo simulation that models with more biased estimates can exhibit lower estimator variance, meaning misspecified models may dominate in both inferential and model selection procedures. These results have direct implications for the replicability and interpretability of linear regression models in psychological research.

articles.title: Anticipatory Threat Disrupts Attention and Working Memory as a Function of Cognitive Anxiety: A Replication and Extension
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; Lou Pardon Tommasini; Gaën Plancher
articles.abstract: Whereas the impact of threat anticipation on attentional resources has been documented, its extension to working memory (WM) had yet to be directly examined. A recent study provided first evidence that anticipating threat impairs WM, and that this impairment increased with cognitive anxiety. However, this study used ambient music inductions prior to each trial, leaving open whether observed costs reflect anticipation per se or music induction. The present study replicated this paradigm using a gamified complex-span task in which participants navigated the rooms of a virtual mansion where a neutral host and a threatening host were said to potentially appear at any time. Critically, no host ever appeared during the task. Music inductions were removed to isolate purely anticipatory processes. The aim was to test whether anticipating threat impaired attentional control and WM, and whether these effects increased with cognitive anxiety. Attentional capture and WM were indexed by parity-judgment and recall accuracy, respectively. A significant interaction with cognitive anxiety emerged, so that threat anticipation impaired both attention and WM at high anxiety. These findings replicate and refine the evidence that anticipatory threat impairs attention and WM depends critically on threat intensity and individual differences in anxiety. Moreover, it introduces a new paradigm for isolating the cognitive costs of threat anticipation.

articles.title: Concern over Mistakes and Personal Standards Across Transdiagnostic Eating Disorder Behavioural Presentations
articles.authors: Chantal P Delaquis; Yasmin Brown; Dean Spirou; Jayanthi Raman; Sylvie Berthoz
articles.abstract:
Concern over Mistakes (CM) reflects a fear of mistakes and harsh self-criticism, while Personal Standards (PS) reflects setting demanding self-imposed standards. These dimensions of perfectionism play distinct yet complementary roles in eating pathology. We aimed to investigate CM and PS across eating disorder (ED) diagnoses and behavioural presentations (restrictive, binge-purge and binge), compared to psychiatric and healthy control (HC) groups. Given the established relationship between negative affect, perfectionism and eating pathology, we controlled for anxiety and depressive symptoms. We expected that CM would not differ between EDs groups, PS would be higher in restricting-type EDs, and all ED groups would score higher than controls.
Participants were drawn from a student/community sample, including 103 with a self-reported lifetime ED, 25 with a non-ED psychiatric diagnosis, and 69 HCs. Separate one-way multivariate analyses of variance (MANOVAs) examined group differences, followed by separate MANCOVAs controlling for anxiety and depressive symptoms.
CM did not significantly differ between ED diagnostic groups or behavioural presentations. All ED groups scored higher than both control groups (ds = 0.94–1.88), except BN, which did not significantly differ from psychiatric controls (d = 0.94). Controlling for negative affect, all behavioural presentation groups remained significantly higher on CM than both control groups (ds = 0.90–1.41). For ED diagnoses, only AN and OSFED scored higher than both controls (ds= 1.27–1.35).
PS also did not significantly differ among ED diagnoses or behavioural presentations. The binge-purge group did not significantly differ from psychiatric controls (d = 0.98). Among diagnostic groups, only AN and OSFED scored higher on PS than both control groups (ds = 1.03–1.07). Anxiety, but not depressive symptoms, was a significant covariate. Controlling for negative affect, only the binge (d = 0.76) and OSFED (d = 0.90) groups scored significantly higher on PS compared to HC.
Our results suggest that CM and PS hold transdiagnostic relevance across EDs. Anxiety symptoms in particular appear to impact the relationship between PS and disordered eating behaviours. Our findings highlight the importance of routinely assessing perfectionism dimensions and anxiety/depressive symptoms to personalize ED treatment approaches.

articles.title: A Tutorial in Dynamic Systems Simulation and Modelling With R, ctsem, and lme4: Couples' Affect Dynamics Over Time
articles.authors: Charles C Driver; Michael Aristodemou
articles.abstract: Understanding how people change is a fundamental goal of psychological science. However, translating complex ideas about psychological dynamics into formal models can be challenging without the right tools. In this tutorial, we introduce a approaches using R and the ctsem package to help researchers build and understand dynamic systems models that capture some of the complexity of psychological processes. We emphasize iterative model-building through simulations, model fitting, and visualizations of the model-implied dynamics alongside their fit to data. We begin with familiar linear models in lme4 and gradually transition to ctsem, which allows us to incorporate complexities such as state-dependent change, random fluctuation distinct from measurement error, covariate effects, interactions, and external inputs. These modelling concepts are illustrated using a running example of affect dynamics in couples therapy, demonstrating how key conceptual and methodological ideas in dynamic systems modelling come together. Our aim is to provide a general framework for understanding dynamic systems modelling and to encourage further exploration of theory-driven statistical approaches in psychological research.

articles.title: When More Is Not Better: Costs of Increasing Multimodal Engagement During Letter–Sound Association Learning
articles.authors: Chotiga Pattamadilok; Lisa Bertolucci; Cyrine Youssef; Felipe Pegado
articles.abstract: Multimodal learning is widely assumed to enhance learning outcomes by engaging multiple sensory and motor systems. However, empirical studies have primarily examined combinations of two modalities, leaving richer learning protocols largely unexplored. This gap is particularly relevant for real-life situations, where several systems typically interact. Literacy acquisition is a prime example, as it requires the integration of visual and auditory input as well as motor representations of letter and speech sound production. To explore the benefits and limits of complex multisensory-motor learning, we investigated how increasing multisensory-motor engagement beyond two systems affects the learning of symbol-sound associations. Specifically, adult participants learned novel pseudoletter-syllable associations under three conditions: bimodal (audio–visual), trimodal (audio–visual–writing), and quadrimodal (audio–visual–writing–speaking). Learning outcomes were assessed using tasks measuring knowledge of pseudoletter–syllable associations, visual perception of pseudoletters, and motor productions of pseudoletters through writing and naming tasks. Contrary to the general predictions of multimodal enrichment theories, performance decreased as the number of modalities increased, consistent with cognitive load accounts suggesting that additional processing demands can impair learning. To further test whether these costs resulted from insufficient processing time, the integration time-window was extended in the second experiment, with the different sensory-motor systems engaged sequentially rather than simultaneously. Under these conditions, the detrimental effect of additional modalities was still present, but the audio–visual–writing training selectively improved pseudoletter writing performance. Together, these findings challenge the common assumption that adding modalities necessarily enhances learning, and suggest that the benefits of multimodal instruction may depend on the balance between representational enrichment and cognitive load. More generally, they highlight important constraints on the implementation of multimodal learnings in educational practices, particularly in early literacy instruction.

articles.title: Positive Mental Health in Families of People with Intellectual Disabilities: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Tianyi Ma; Vasiliki Totsika; Menglong Bao; Caitlin Williams
articles.abstract:
Abstract 
Background: Research on families of people with intellectual disabilities has traditionally focused on negative aspects of mental health. A scoping review of studies on positive mental health aimed to map existing operationalisations, correlates, and methods used.
Method: We searched Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ProQuest Dissertation, EThOS and Google Scholar for quantitative studies on positive mental health. Findings were mapped on a multi-dimensional framework developed from existing models and evidence.  
Results: Positive mental health was most commonly operationalised as emotional and psychological well-being, with fewer studies examining social or existential well-being. Most frequently researched correlates were psychological resources of caregivers, behaviours of individuals with intellectual disabilities, and social support.
Conclusions: Research on positive mental health has increased but it still weighs heavily towards emotional and psychological well-being, individual-level correlates, and mothers. More research is needed on relational and existential well-being, fathers, siblings, grandparents and the role of contextual factors, services and policies.

articles.title: Adaptive multi-frequency oscillator modeling of coordination recovery during rhythm switching in human musical quartets
articles.authors: Bavo Van Kerrebroeck; Alexander Pantelis Demos; Marc Leman; Marcelo Wanderley; Caroline Palmer; Pieter-Jan Maes
articles.abstract: Musical ensemble coordination requires groups to stabilize shared timing while adapting to perturbations and changing rhythmic constraints. We developed an adaptive multi-frequency oscillator model of how human quartets recover coordination during switches between binary and ternary meters. The model combines nonlinear phase coupling, Hebbian-like frequency adaptation, and resonance-dependent relaxation in a four-oscillator network, allowing individual tempo adaptation while preserving subgroup-specific coupling within and between dyads. We evaluated the model against empirical quartet performances and surrogate datasets in which interpersonal coordination structure was disrupted. Parameter optimization minimized discrepancies between empirical and simulated inter-onset intervals, pairwise asynchronies, and cluster phase dynamics. Simulations reproduced transient destabilization after perturbation cues followed by recovery toward a new coordinated state. Cross-validated mixed-effects analyses showed that the model fit empirical quartets better than surrogate quartets, indicating sensitivity to genuine human coordination structure and generalization to unseen data. Optimized parameters revealed condition-specific mechanisms: within-dyad coupling was reduced in Complex–Ternary rhythms, whereas between-dyad coupling was lowest in Complex–Binary rhythms. Frequency relaxation rates were higher in Complex than Simple rhythms across meters, suggesting stronger adaptive tempo correction during polyrhythmic coordination. Stability analyses revealed bounded regions of period and phase synchronization, including Arnold tongue-like entrainment regions shaped by coupling architecture, adaptation asymmetry, and meter ratio. Together, these findings show that quartet synchronization depends on interactions among interpersonal coupling, adaptive frequency regulation, resonance-dependent constraints, and rhythmic ratio constraints. The model provides an interpretable dynamical framework for understanding how human groups recover, maintain, and reorganize coordinated behavior under changing rhythmic demands.

articles.title: Return to work after mild stroke in adults aged 18-64: A qualitative study
articles.authors: Bénédicte Dussault; Laurie Dubois; Marie-Christine Ouellet; Simon Beaulieu-Bonneau
articles.abstract:
Objective. This qualitative study aimed to describe the return to work (RTW) experience of adults aged 18 to 64 who had experienced a mild stroke in Québec. More specifically, inspired by the Adaptiveness-Purposefulness-Cooperativeness model, the study sought to identify the factors related to the person, the workplace, and healthcare services which may constitute barriers or facilitators to RTW in this population.
Methods. This study used a qualitative design. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with thirteen adults (10 women; ages 36 to 61; 13 to 24 months post-stroke). 
Results. A content analysis revealed that person-related factors included the presence and intensity of post-stroke symptoms, self-awareness and readiness to RTW, coping strategies, motivation, financial and social resources, and personal characteristics. Workplace factors included formal and informal accommodations, interpersonal aspects and employment conditions. Factors related to health services included adapted medical accommodations and medical follow-up, access to supportive care services (functional and psychological support), as well as recognition of patient’s condition and needs. 
Conclusions. The study confirms certain factors proposed in the existing literature, highlighting those specific to a population that often present fewer post-stroke impairments and rarely receives rehabilitation services. All these factors must be considered to provide more appropriate healthcare services, to guide workplaces in the type of support they can offer, and to assist individual in their recovery and RTW following a mild stroke.

articles.title: Cardio-respiratory modulation of arousal and excitability states
articles.authors: Teresa Berther; Martina Saltafossi; Daniel Kluger
articles.abstract: The field of interoception research is currently working towards an understanding of how brain-body states determine human perception, cognition, and behaviour. Recent studies suggest that transient dynamics of arousal neuromodulation and cortical excitability are of particular interest. In this Perspective Article, we succinctly review the current evidence for cardio-respiratory modulation of arousal and excitability states in the human brain. We outline the systematic relationships of both cardiac and respiratory rhythms to non-invasive readouts such as changes in pupil diameter as well as (a)periodic neural signatures of excitability. Integrating these single-domain findings, we suggest a path towards a multi-organ perspective of brain-body neuroscience.

articles.title: Introducing openESM: A database of openly available experience sampling datasets
articles.authors: Björn S. Siepe; Jonas M B Haslbeck; Matthias Kloft; Anabel Büchner; Yong Zhang; Eiko I Fried; Daniel W. Heck
articles.abstract: Experience sampling via mobile devices enables unprecedented insights into daily life. However, individual studies often cannot answer research questions conclusively, and open data are scattered across repositories in different formats. This impedes research into robustness, generalizability, and heterogeneity. We address this issue by introducing openESM, an open-source database of openly available experience sampling datasets in a harmonized format. The growing database currently comprises 60 datasets with more than 16,000 participants and more than 740,000 observations. Metadata can be searched via our website (openesmdata.org) to select and download datasets via packages in R and Python. We demonstrate the potential of openESM through an analysis of within-person correlations of positive and negative affect in 39 datasets, providing evidence for a large negative momentary correlation (-0.49, 95% CI: [-0.54, -0.42]). We end by discussing the design principles that will allow openESM to become a continuously evolving community resource for cumulative experience sampling research.

articles.title: BoundIRT: An R Package for Bounded Continuous Item Response Theory with Factor Score Regression
articles.authors: Dylan Molenaar
articles.abstract: In various research settings, responses to questionnaire items are continuously distributed and bounded from below and above. Suitable item response theory (IRT) models are available for the response data; however, implementations of these models differ significantly in their estimation method, availability, and user-friendliness. These differences hamper the application of such models in general, and model fit comparison in particular. Therefore, in this paper, BoundIRT is presented, which implements four popular bounded IRT models from the literature in the R statistical computing environment. The package provides various facilities for model estimation and model fit assessment. In addition, once a suitable model has been established for a given dataset, the factor score regression facilities can be used to conduct regression analyses of the latent variable in the model with respect to other variables.

articles.title: Shared Reality, Perceived Responsiveness and Interpersonal Emotion Regulation Among Parents-Adolescents Dyads
articles.authors: Roni Yuval; Reuma Gadassi Polack; Hadas Wiseman; Haran Sened
articles.abstract: Shared reality is an experience of having "merged minds" and shared inner states, e.g. feelings, thoughts, opinions and concerns with a close relationship partner. It is a substantial component for establishing and nurturing close relationships. The purpose of this study was to examine, for the first time, shared reality between parents and children. To this day, the focus of research in this field was on romantic couples and adult strangers. We investigated 60 dyads of parents of adolescent children (ages 9-17) through self-report questionnaires and experience sampling methods, completed by parents 3 times a day for 3 days (K=728 questionnaires). Stronger parent-child shared reality was found to be associated with more perceived responsiveness experienced by the parent from the child, and with more interpersonal emotion regulation behaviors performed by the parent towards the child. The associations remained when controlling for parent-child closeness and for parent shared reality with their partner. Together, these findings suggest that shared reality is a significant and valuable factor within parent-adolescent relationships, with unique relevance beyond other relationship components. Our findings demonstrate how the unique shared reality between children and parents can be an essential part of the family’s everyday life.

articles.title: Cognitive maps are flexible, dynamic, (re)constructed representations
articles.authors: Aidan J Horner; James A. Ainge; Alexander Easton; Simon J James; Jeremy Kendal; John Sutton; Jan Wiener
articles.abstract: Spatial navigation is the ability to purposefully move from one location to another. Central to many theories of navigation is the proposal that we build a ‘cognitive map’ of our external environment. We identify three conceptions of cognitive maps, from highly coherent long-term representations of space to more fragmentary representations. Reviewing the literature, we show that many navigation behaviours thought to require a cognitive map can be supported by the interaction of specific navigation strategies with minimal, fragmentary knowledge of the environment. Further, we argue that the range of navigation behaviours, strategies, individual differences, and navigational aids and systems used during navigation point toward representations that are more flexible than any of the three main conceptions of a cognitive map allow. We propose that spatial knowledge is stored in a more fragmentary manner but, critically, more complex representations are (re)constructed dynamically in the given navigational moment. The form and complexity of these constructed representations are tightly connected to the dynamic interaction between the navigator, including the strategies and aids they are using, and the environment. We link this proposal to the literature on spatially tuned neurons in the medial temporal lobes, emphasising that the heterogeneity of these functional neurons and their adaptation to changes in environmental structure and navigational goals supports our proposal that cognitive maps are dynamically (re)constructed representations. Therefore, cognitive maps are not relatively coherent, stable representations of spatial environments, but instead are dynamically and flexibly (re)constructed representations of the given navigational moment.

articles.title: The Association Between SES and Students’ Achievement Motivation in Secondary School: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis Spanning Two Decades of PISA Data
articles.authors: Sarah Grünthal; Lena Keller; Julia Kretschmann; Hanna Dumont; Martin Brunner
articles.abstract: Major theoretical frameworks of achievement motivation link family socioeconomic status (SES) to students’ achievement motivation in school settings. However, systematic evidence on this association remains limited. This study presents the first meta-analysis on this topic, using representative individual participant data (IPD) from the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA). The analysis included 485 student samples comprising a total of 3,576,278 15-year-old students, spanning four SES indicators, eight achievement motivation components, four academic domains, 92 countries, and eight assessment cycles across more than two decades (2000–2022). The average meta-analytic association between SES and achievement motivation was small (r = .10, 95% CI [.09, .11]), indicating slightly higher achievement motivation among students from higher-SES families.
