articles.abstract: Purpose: Simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use is a common type of polysubstance use amongyoung adults. Depending on the substance used first, the amount of alcohol consumed might vary.Coping or enhancement motives endorsed on simultaneous use days might also impact alcoholconsumption differently. This study examined whether alcohol use differed on alcohol-only versussimultaneous use days, and whether using alcohol versus cannabis first on a simultaneous use daypredicted heavier alcohol consumption. We also examined whether differences in alcoholconsumption depended on daily levels of coping or enhancement motives.Methods: Undergraduate students (n = 370; Mage=20.8; SD = 1.5) completed a 14-weekend daily diarystudy in Fall 2021. Surveys administered Friday to Sunday mornings measured alcohol use, cannabisuse, their order of use, number of drinks consumed, and motives for simultaneous use. Analyseswere restricted to alcohol-only and simultaneous use days (n = 2826/9017; 31.3%).Results: Multilevel models showed that students consumed more alcohol on simultaneous use days(Mdrinks=5.08) than alcohol-only days (Mdrinks=4.23). Students also consumed about 1.4 fewer drinkswhen cannabis was used first compared to when alcohol was used first on simultaneous use days.However, the effect of order of use on alcohol consumption did not depend on daily levels ofcoping or enhancement motives.Conclusions: Using cannabis first on simultaneous use days was associated with less drinking, aneffect not apparently linked to situational drinking motives. Contextual factors associated withcannabis use such as affect (e.g., negative or positive) and setting (e.g., alone or with others) mayexplain lighter drinking on cannabis-first simultaneous use days.

articles.title: Toddlers recognize words in an unfamiliar accent after brief exposure
articles.authors: Rachel Schmale; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract:
Both subjective impressions and previous research with monolingual listeners suggest that a foreign accent interferes with word recognition in infants, young children, and adults. However, because being exposed to multiple accents is likely to be an everyday occurrence in many societies, it is unexpected that such non-standard pronunciations would significantly impede language processing once the listener has experience with the relevant accent. Indeed, we report that 24-month-olds successfully accommodate an unfamiliar accent in rapid word learning after less than 2 minutes of accent exposure. These results underline the robustness of our speech perception mechanisms, which allow listeners to adapt even in the absence of extensive lexical knowledge and clear known-word referents.

A video abstract of this article can be viewed at http: ⁄ ⁄www.youtube.com ⁄watch?v=bYnaZkMyKtY&feature=youtu.be

articles.title: ProQOL Factor Structure in Creative Arts and Psychomotor Therapies: Cross-Validated CFA and ESEM Evidence
articles.authors: Harm Damen; Jackie Heijman; Fenja; Suzanne Haeyen
articles.abstract: The Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL) is widely used to monitor compassion satisfaction, burnout, and secondary traumatic stress, yet its latent structure has not been examined in creative arts and psychomotor therapies (CAPTs). In a national Dutch CAPTs survey (N = 598), we tested whether the three-subscale ProQOL framework remains supported using split-sample cross-validation. The sample was randomly split (Sample A, n = 316; Sample B, n = 282). In each half, we estimated strict 3-factor confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and 3-factor exploratory structural equation model (ESEM) with WLSMV estimation. Bifactor models were sensitivity analyses only. We also examined measurement invariance, factor similarity, and internal consistency. In both subsamples, strict CFA showed inadequate fit (CFI ≤ .887; RMSEA ≥ .078), whereas 3-factor ESEM showed acceptable fit (CFI ≥ .956; RMSEA ≤ .053) and replicated across halves. Multigroup analyses supported metric and scalar invariance. Factor similarity was high (Tucker’s φ = .92–.98), and internal consistency of the three subscales was strong (McDonald’s ω = .81–.93). Loadings indicated a coherent compassion satisfaction dimension with burnout-secondary traumatic stress overlap, reverse-scored burnout items loading primarily as inverse compassion satisfaction rather than burnout, and known low-loading boundary items, consistent with prior evidence. The better fit of ESEM relative to strict CFA indicates that three-subscale scoring remains reasonably supported for research and practice in CAPTs despite item-level limitations. Invariance, factor similarity, and internal consistency further supported this conclusion. When modelling ProQOL structure, analyses should allow cross-loadings instead of the manual’s zero-cross-loading specification alone.

articles.title: De Novo Motor Learning as Controller Synthesis: A Conceptual Framework
articles.authors: Ian S. Howard
articles.abstract:
Most studies of human motor learning focus on adaptation, in which an existing controller is recalibrated after changes in dynamics, kinematics, or sensory feedback. In these paradigms, relevant control variables, coordinate representations, and feedback organization are taken as available a priori, and learning is described as tuning parameters within an already specified controller architecture. However, de novo motor-learning tasks require learners to establish novel relationships between intention, sensory feedback, and action, rather than recalibrating a familiar controller. These tasks often show slow or variable acquisition, limited but structured generalization, strong context dependence, and dissociations between learning rate and final performance. Such features are difficult to explain solely as parameter tuning within a fixed controller architecture.

Here we propose that de novo motor learning is better understood as controller synthesis, rather than only as parameter adaptation. On this view, learning involves forming and stabilizing content-addressable, plant-state-addressed controller memories: local sensorimotor control organizations that specify where a controller applies, which task-relevant signals are selected and routed, how state and progress are estimated, how control is computed, how internal control signals map onto action, and when and how the controller is expressed. This framework interprets slow acquisition, limited generalization, context dependence, and learning-rate/outcome dissociations as possible consequences of uncertainty about controller-memory structure, rather than slow parameter convergence within an established controller. It also suggests tests for distinguishing controller synthesis from fixed-structure adaptation, contextual inference, and policy-learning accounts.

articles.title: Relations between Parenting Practices in Adolescence and Daily Life Emotional Processes in Early Adulthood
articles.authors: Ercan Ozdemir; Aja Louise Murray; Luke Power; Zhuoni Xiao; Manuel Eisner; Denis Ribeaud; Xinxin Zhu
articles.abstract:
Background. Adolescent parenting experiences have enduring implications for emotional functioning in adulthood, yet the dynamic regulatory mechanisms through which these effects operate in daily life remain poorly understood. 
Methods. Using a longitudinal design, parenting exposure trajectories from age 13 to age 17 were identified via latent class growth analysis (LCGA) on three-wave assessment of authoritarian parenting and parental support (N = 451). Following exclusions for class assignment certainty and ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data density, multilevel vector autoregressive network analysis (mlVAR) was applied to 14-day EMA data (N = 270; 4 beeps/day) across the LCGA-defined parenting exposure classes to estimate temporal and contemporaneous networks of perceived stress, hostile affect, rumination and suppression.
Results. We identified four parenting exposure classes involving Supportive (low authoritarian-high support), Controlling-Supportive (moderate authoritarian-high support), authoritarian (high authoritarian-low support) and Moderate (mid-level on both dimensions).  Higher parental support was associated with looser contemporaneous and temporal network density, indicating affective system flexibility, whereas authoritarian parenting was related to rigidity, marked by more persistent hostility and a more pronounced effect of rumination on concurrent affective dynamics. 
Conclusion. Our results highlight the enduring day-to-day affective functioning correlates of the adolescent family environment on emotional outcomes in the transition to adulthood delineating the differential impact of distinct parenting practices.

articles.title: The Explicit Anchor: How Inferential Reasoning Mimics Introspective Access in Implicit Evaluation Prediction
articles.authors: Yahel Nudler; Adam Morris; Benedek Kurdi
articles.abstract: Do individuals possess introspective access to their implicit evaluations? Although recent research shows that people can often predict their scores on indirect measures, it remains unclear whether this effect reflects genuine introspection or inferential reasoning. We tested an anchoring-and-adjustment account, proposing that individuals predict implicit evaluations by anchoring on accessible explicit evaluations and then adjusting based on available information, such as cultural knowledge. Across three experiments (N = 3,182), we used a relational evaluative conditioning paradigm with novel nonwords to isolate explicit evaluations as the primary source for inference. Manipulating the align-ment between explicit and implicit evaluations, between or within participants, yielded consistent support for the anchoring-and-adjustment hypothesis. Predictions were accurate only when explicit evaluations provided a valid cue; when the two dissociated, accuracy fell systematically below chance. These findings suggest that knowledge of one’s implicit evaluations is dominantly derived from explicit cues rather than discovered through direct introspection.

articles.title: Semantic Interference in Blocked-Cyclic Word Production with Different Stimulus Types, Tasks, and Response Modalities
articles.authors: Stefan Wöhner; Andreas Widmann; Sophia Forchner; Erich Schröger; Jörg D. Jescheniak
articles.abstract: Blocked-cyclic picture naming is a prominent tool in word production research. Responses were slower when the stimuli were presented blocked by semantic category than when they are presented intermixed. Wöhner et al. (2021) extended the task to sound naming and found that the semantic interference was much larger in sound naming (e.g., a barking) than in picture naming (e.g., of a dog), by a factor of approximately three, even when the same words were produced (e.g., “dog”). We explored possible reasons for this differential interference pattern. We replicated the differential interference when the stimuli were presented briefly, ruling out that it results from substantial overlap between stimulus processing on the one hand and phonological response preparation and pre-articulatory self-monitoring on the other. In contrast, we found similar-sized interference when the sounds and pictures were replaced with spoken and written words to which participants responded with the translation in their second language, ruling out that the differential interference results from different input modalities. We also observed the differential interference in sound and picture naming when the spoken response was replaced with a typed response, ruling out that it results from a specific (spoken) response modality. Overall, the data demonstrate the robustness of the differential interference in sound and picture naming and provide evidence that the semantic interference in blocked-cyclic naming is effectively shaped by early stimulus-specific perceptual and semantic – “lead-in” – processes, which precede lexical selection. These early processes require more attention in word production research.

articles.title: Acoustic-Phonetic Differences between Infant- and Adult-directed Speech: The Role of Stress and Utterance Position
articles.authors: Alex Eguiluz; Yuanyuan Wang; Amanda Seidl; Alejandrina Cristia
articles.abstract:
Previous studies have shown that infant-directed speech (IDS) differs from adultdirected
speech (ADS) on a variety of dimensions. The aim of the current study was
to investigate whether acoustic differences between IDS and ADS in English are
modulated by prosodic structure. We compared vowels across the two registers (IDS,
ADS) in both stressed and unstressed syllables, and in both utterance-medial and -
final positions. Vowels in target bisyllabic trochees in the speech of twenty mothers
of four- and eleven-month-olds were analyzed. While stressed and unstressed vowels
differed between IDS and ADS for a measure of F0, and trended in similar directions
for vowel peripherality, neither set differed in duration. These profiles held for both
utterance-medial and -final words.

articles.title: Evidence accumulation modeling of learning, repetition, and control adaptation processes in Stroop and contingency learning
articles.authors: Sven Wientjes; Clay B. Holroyd
articles.abstract: Sequential effects in the Stroop task arise from multiple adaptive processes, including conflict adaptation and contingency learning. Standard analyses typically operationalize these processes using regressors encoding events such as recent or frequent congruency and response contingencies. However, because adaptation unfolds over multiple trials, such analyses provide only a partial characterization and may produce spurious effects when multiple processes operate simultaneously. We address this problem using a Bayesian generative model of evidence accumulation that tracks multiple latent expectations. Iterative cycles of model criticism and extension reveal that sequential effects in the contingency learning task are best described as a combination of processes, including stimulus-response contingency learning in tandem with a more strategic signaling effect. We show that these processes can mimic conflict adaptation effects found in the Stroop task. However, the model’s trial‑level characterization of sequential dynamics helps dissociate these processes from pure conflict adaptation processes, revealing two additional updating mechanisms—sequential and item‑specific conflict adaptation—which are detectable even in a highly controlled confound minimized design. More broadly, we argue that analyses of multi-trial sequential data should be accompanied by posterior predictive model criticism, as significance tests on history-dependent regressors cannot by themselves rule out misspecified accounts of the observed dynamics.

articles.title: Imagining the Future: Modality Effects of Mental Imagery, Verbal Reasoning, and Virtual Reality on Behavioural Engagement Predictions in Dysphoria
articles.authors: Eleanor Burton; Matthew Coxon; Jennifer Shevchenko
articles.abstract: Difficulties anticipating and engaging in future activities are characteristic of dysphoria and depression. This research investigated whether simulating future activities could improve prospective evaluations of behavioural engagement, and whether increasing immersion enhanced these effects. Across two studies, participants completed mental imagery, verbal reasoning, or (in Study 2) virtual reality tasks while evaluating future activities. In Study 1, both mental imagery and verbal reasoning improved perceived likelihood of engagement, importance, vividness, anticipatory pleasure, and mood. Mental imagery showed some selective advantages for vividness and anticipatory pleasure, although verbal reasoning produced broadly comparable effects. Study 2 introduced a virtual reality condition to examine whether greater immersion would strengthen these outcomes. Contrary to predictions, virtual reality did not produce additional benefits over mental imagery or verbal reasoning. All three tasks improved prospective evaluations across most measures, while mental imagery and verbal reasoning were more effective than virtual reality in increasing motivation. Participants in the verbal reasoning condition also reported similar levels of imagery use to those in the imagery condition, suggesting spontaneous imagery engagement. Overall, findings suggest that engaging in structured future-oriented thinking, regardless of modality, can positively influence expectations about future activities. The results suggest that simply engaging in the structured, deliberate simulation of future events, regardless of the specific technique used, may be sufficient to produce change. These findings have implications for low-cost cognitive interventions aimed at improving motivation and behavioural engagement in dysphoria.

articles.title: Substitute or Extension: Why Some Turn to Virtual Partners and What It Reveals About Their Personality and Mating Psychology
articles.authors: Desiree Popelka; christine mohr; Bruno Lemaitre
articles.abstract: Increasingly more people outsource their intimate needs for romantic and social interactions from real-life to artificial. The virtual relationship, also called virtual romance services (VRS), encompasses simulated romantic companionship with paid human online models (e.g. OnlyFans Girlfriend/ Boyfriend Experience, etc.) or with non-human AI chatbots (e.g. Replika, ChatGPT). We investigated i) what characterizes individuals who use virtual partners, and ii) whether these virtual relationships are a substitute for unsuccessful mating attempts, or simply an extension of existing mating activity in real life. Data were collected via an online survey assessing personality traits, mating-related characteristics, and mating effort in German-speaking respondents from Switzerland (March 2025) and Germany (December 2025). The combined sample consisted of 183 current virtual relationships users and 1’871 never users. Findings indicated that virtual relationships represent an extension of existing mating activity rather than a substitute for failed real-life mating attempts. In addition, users as compared to never users scored lower in Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Partner Investment, but higher in Narcissism, Partner Upgrading, and Mate Locating. While virtual relationships use remains a scientifically understudied phenomenon, the present study challenges the widespread cultural assumption that those who engage with virtual partners are socially withdrawn and romantically unsuccessful, suggesting instead that use may be driven by intrinsic personality characteristics and an underlying short-term mating orientation.

articles.title: Development of infants’ segmentation of words from native speech: a meta-analytic approach
articles.authors: Christina Bergmann; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: Infants start learning words, the building blocks of language, at least by 6 months. To do so, they must be able to extract the phonological form of words from running speech. A rich literature has investigated this process, termed word segmentation. We addressed the fundamental question of how infants of different ages segment words from their native language using a meta-analytic approach. Based on previous popular theoretical and experimental work, we expected infants to display familiarity preferences early on, with a switch to novelty preferences as infants become more proficient at processing and segmenting native speech. We also considered the possibility that this switch may occur at different points in time as a function of infants’ native language and took into account the impact of various task- and stimulus-related factors that might affect difficulty. The combined results from 168 experiments reporting on data gathered from 3774 infants revealed a persistent familiarity preference across all ages. There was no significant effect of additional factors, including native language and experiment design. Further analyses revealed no sign of selective data collection or reporting. We conclude that models of infant information processing that are frequently cited in this domain may not, in fact, apply in the case of segmenting words from native speech.

articles.title: Separating visual memories through learned action associations
articles.authors: Caterina Trentin; Christian Nicolas Leon Olivers; Heleen A Slagter
articles.abstract: What organizing principles govern visual memory? Perceptual feature similarity and semantic relatedness have long been considered the primary candidates. Previous theoretical work, however, suggests that the similarity of actions used to interact with objects may constitute a more fundamental organizing principle. Here, we test whether similarity in learned action associations shapes the representational structure of visual memories. Across two experiments (N = 48 each), participants memorized the orientations of two bars and reproduced them by performing a cued action (grip or slide). Critically, across trials, stimulus-action mappings were stable for some stimulus pairs but varied randomly for oth-ers. We found that objects associated with different actions were remembered as more visually distinct, and this representational repulsion was amplified when action mappings were consistent and learned by participants. These findings indicate that stable action rela-tionships shape visual memory representations, supporting the view that similarity in action association constitutes a key organizing dimension of representational structure.

articles.title: Neuromodulation for hearing and listening: Current perspectives and future opportunities
articles.authors: Jessica Pepper; Kate Slade; Chris Plack; Helen Nuttall
articles.abstract:
Non-invasive brain stimulation techniques, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial electrical stimulation, have been instrumental in the establishment of causal links between a specific behavioural function and the cortical region or neural oscillation governing such functions. Whilst much non-invasive brain stimulation research has been conducted within motor and visual domains, arguably less is known as to how non-invasive brain stimulation can be used to functionally modulate auditory and speech brain areas to influence perception. Non-invasive brain stimulation to auditory cortex has the potential to revolutionise our understanding of how the brain processes acoustic information, and to be implemented in new treatments for auditory disorders. Despite this utility, the optimal parameters implemented to excite or inhibit auditory cortical activity remains a significant debate amongst auditory neuroscientists, particularly due to variability arising from initial brain states and individual differences. 
This review provides a comprehensive account of how non-invasive brain stimulation to auditory cortical networks has been applied to study basic and high-level auditory processing, as well as a critical evaluation of the protocols used in previous research. Crucially, directions for future research are discussed, such as the prospect of implementing multiple non-invasive brain stimulation and neuroimaging techniques in conjunction, and advancements in closed-loop stimulation. Furthermore, the clinical implications that neuromodulation of auditory cortex may have for people with listening difficulties will be explored, highlighting the scalable opportunities to reach patients outside of traditional healthcare contexts. It is concluded that whilst more research should be conducted with larger sample sizes and personalised stimulation protocols, there is great promise in the application of non-invasive brain stimulation to auditory cortex for enhancing listening ability across the lifespan and across clinical conditions.

articles.title: Measuring language development from child-centered recordings
articles.authors: Yaya Sy; William N. Havard; Lavechin; Emmanuel Dupoux; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract:
Standard ways to measure child language development from spontaneous corpora rely on detailed linguistic descriptions of a language as well as exhaustive transcriptions of the child’s speech, which today can only be done through costly human labor. We tackle both issues by proposing (1) a new language development metric (based on entropy) that does not require linguistic knowledge other than having a corpus of text in the language in question to train a language model, (2) a method to derive this metric directly from speech based on a smaller text-speech parallel corpus. Here, we present descriptive results on an open archive including data from six Englishlearning children as a proof of concept. We document that our entropy metric documents a gradual convergence of children’s speech towards adults’ speech as a function of age, and it also correlates moderately with lexical and morphosyntactic measures derived from morphologically parsed transcriptions.
The source code of the experiments is released at https://github.com/yaya-sy/EntropyBasedCLDMetrics
Index Terms: L1 acquisition, child speech, morphosyntax, phonetics, speech technology application

articles.title: Introducing GenAI to assessment in Higher Education risks the social contract between staff and students: a qualitative study
articles.authors: Lyba Razzaq; Isla Fay; Deborah Talmi; Roni Tibon; Maryam Abo-Tabik; Alexandru Marcoci; Giulio Corsi; Sarah N. Mattey; Georgiana Thorpe-Apreutesei; Yael Benn
articles.abstract: While perspectives on the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in assessment in higher education have been widely reported, less is known about discipline-specific concern. Here we focus on Psychology, where essays are central to assessment and require context-dependent judgement, critical evaluation, synthesis of evidence, and scientific reasoning. To ensure that findings reflect shared, cross-institution concerns in this discipline, we conducted semi-structured focus groups with Psychology students (N = 11) and staff (N = 14) from three UK universities differing in geographical location and entry-requirements. Discussions explored views on GenAI in HE for assessment, including reactions to examples comparing human and AI-generated feedback. Thematic analysis identified three themes: (1) Human-Machine Ambiguity, (2) Overreliance, Weakening Cognition and the Value of Education, and (3) The Social Contract: Personal and Interpersonal Values. Consistent with previous research, participants raised concerns about ethics, fairness, data integrity, and the impact on learning and cognition. Extending existing literature, findings highlight concerns about the erosion of trust and the social contract underpinning higher education, which could threaten the experience of staff and students. With its focus on essays in assessment, psychology provides a strong test case for examining the views of staff and students on AI-grading more generally.

articles.title: Occupational Stigma and the Dehumanization of Dirty Workers: Emotional and Behavioral Mechanisms
articles.authors: Elsa Boulard; Roberta Rosa Valtorta; CRISTINA BALDISSARRI; Christophe Demarque; Valerie Fointiat; LUCA ANDRIGHETTO
articles.abstract:
Recent literature suggests that dirty jobs, that is occupations perceived as physically, socially or morally tainted, foster distinct processes of workers’ dehumanization: biologization, objectification, and animalization, respectively. However, little is known about the psychological mechanisms associated with these processes. To address this gap, we conducted a preliminary and three preregistered studies testing a theoretical model linking occupational taint to emotional reactions, dehumanizing perceptions, and behavioral intentions. Study 1 (N = 484) identified physically, socially, and morally tainted occupations in the French context, testing the generalization of previous classifications. Studies 2 (N = 299) and 3 (N = 433) supported distinct dehumanization pathways, while showing that emotions played a partial role and that morally tainted occupations were associated with the strongest emotional and behavioral hostility. 
This research advances dirty work literature by highlighting the complexity of occupational dehumanization and the need for further investigation across jobs, contexts, and psychological levels.

articles.title: The acoustic properties of bilingual infant-directed speech
articles.authors: Kyle Danielson; Amanda Seidl; k onishi; Golnoush Alamian; Alejandrina Cristia; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract: Does the acoustic input for bilingual infants equal the conjunction of the input heard by monolinguals of each separate language? The present letter tackles this question, focusing on maternal speech addressed to 11-month-old infants, on the cusp of perceptual attunement. The acoustic characteristics of the point vowels /a,i,u/ were measured in the spontaneous infant-directed speech of French-English bilingual mothers, as well as in the speech of French and English monolingual mothers. Bilingual caregivers produced their two languages with acoustic-prosodic separation equal to that of the monolinguals, while also conveying distinct spectral characteristics of the point vowels in their two languages.

articles.title: Meta-Objectification and Work Features:  A Meta-Analysis of Their Impact on Self-Objectification in the Workplace
articles.authors: Elsa Boulard; Adrien Alejandro Fillon; CRISTINA BALDISSARRI; Valerie Fointiat; Christophe Demarque; LUCA ANDRIGHETTO
articles.abstract: A great amount of research highlights self-objectification—perceiving oneself more as an object than a full human being—as a growing concern given its negative implications for employees’ well-being and organizational effectiveness. However, the specific impact of work-related antecedents on self-objectification and its forms remains unclear. To address this, we conducted a meta-analysis (n = 19, k = 99) on the relationship between key triggers (meta-objectification and work features) and forms of self-objectification (instrumentalization and denial of humanness), drawing on empirical studies involving 7781 participants (Mage = 31.11, SDage = 7.08) from diverse professional and cultural contexts. We identified strong associations between meta-objectification and instrumentalization (ρ = .70), as well as between objectifying work features and denial of humanness (ρ = .51). While the perception of being objectified by others, i.e. meta-objectification, is predominantly associated with the perceptions of being a tool, repetitiveness, fragmentation, and other-direction, i.e. objectifying work features, are closely tied to diminished attribution of cognitive and emotional capabilities. Further moderation analyses highlighted variations based on population type, study design, and geographical context. This research advances the theoretical understanding of working objectification by disentangling its antecedents and mechanisms, underscoring the need for targeted interventions to reduce workplace dehumanization.

articles.title: Twin Analyses Without Zygosity Information: The Promise and Pitfalls of the Normal Finite-Mixture-Distribution Twin Model
articles.authors: Madelief Isabel Kuijper; Camiel M. van der Laan; Abe Dirk Hofman; Elsje van Bergen; Bruno Sauce
articles.abstract: Twin designs offer a powerful framework for disentangling genetic and environmental sources of individual differences, but require zygosity information that is often unavailable. When zygosity is unknown, analyses may still be possible using a normal finite-mixture-distribution model. This model assumes that the bivariate twin phenotype is normally distributed within each zygosity group, an assumption that cannot be directly verified because zygosity is unobserved. We conducted a simulation study to determine how well the normal finite-mixture-distribution model recovered parameters if this assumption is violated and if the twin difference distribution could serve as a diagnostic for violations. In univariate and bivariate simulations, we varied sample size, variance structure and the degree and source of kurtosis. We examined whether marginal score transformations reduce bias. We applied univariate and bivariate models to educational gaming data with unknown zygosity. Simulation estimates were most precise at high heritability and remained reasonably stable with samples as small as 200 pairs. Excess kurtosis in twin difference scores substantially biased estimates, and marginal transformations did not meaningfully reduce bias. Kurtosis-related bias was smaller in the bivariate model than in the univariate model. Empirical estimates based on the univariate model seemed highly biased, producing very high heritability estimates (0.91–0.99), except for the measure of division-skills (A = 0.58, C= 0, E= 0.42). Estimates based on the bivariate model seemed less biased, but unstable. Although mixture modelling may be used for twin-analyses without zygosity information, violations of bivariate normality may introduce considerable, difficult-to-detect bias, warranting careful interpretation of results.

articles.title: The Neurocomputational Underpinnings of Psychological and Behavioral Responses to Unintended Harm
articles.authors: Elijah Paul Galvan; Jeroen M van Baar; Luke J. Chang; Alan Sanfey
articles.abstract: A crucial feature of human social cohesion is a feeling of responsibility when we cause harm to others, and an associated willingness to repair any damage we have caused. However, it is largely unknown to what degree these tendencies are evident when the harm we cause has been unintentional.  Do we provide reparations to rectify the unintended consequences of the actions? In the current study we explore this question, focusing on the role of responsibility as a potential motivator of reparative behavior. In a novel, incentive-compatible, group decision-making task, we addressed these questions by leveraging both computational modeling and functional neuroimaging. In our sample (N = 48), we found that feelings of responsibility for inflicting unintended harm were computationally tractable: a group’s collective responsibility reflected the psychophysics of diminishing sensitivity, diffused solely over those who were accountable for inflicting the harm, and was agnostic to dissenting votes. We found evidence that these feelings of responsibility were encoded in several regions of the brain, including the orbitofrontal cortex, the posterior cingulate cortex, and the amygdala. In terms of reparative action, individual preferences for rectifying harm predicted decisions to subsequently repair harm, irrespective of whether the individual themselves caused it.

articles.title: Designing an intergenerational Dance for Health programme: Perspectives from younger and older urban Swiss adults
articles.authors: Courtney Casale; Ryssa Moffat; Maylin Demir; Chantal Nagel; Emily S. Cross
articles.abstract: Dance for Health programmes have shown promise in supporting the wellbeing of older adults. Yet to fully capitalise upon the value of such programmes for community members, rich opportunities exist to develop participant-tailored classes and to incorporate intergenerational interactions. Here, we took a qualitative approach to gain a deeper understanding of urban Swiss older and younger adults’ expectations and desires for an intergenerational dance programme to support various components of psychosocial and physical wellbeing. Focus group members (N = 21; 15 older adults: 76.13 ± 4.12 years, 6 younger adults: 23.83 ± 3.06 years) engaged in a guided discussion about design elements of such a programme. The discussion focussed on themes related to wellbeing, dance class elements, programme logistics, social interactions, and potential barriers to participation. We used deductive and inductive techniques to analyse the discussions. Deductively, we evaluated 11 concrete design elements (class size, class length/frequency, total duration, location, facility, time/days, dance style, music type, learning materials, advertising, social interactions). Inductively, we identified a central theme of ‘Feeding the Soul’, characterising focus group members’ emphasis on the value of a positive peer group dynamic, a supportive learning environment, personal wellbeing, and inclusivity. Overall, focus group members expressed a preference for activities that offer psychosocial fulfilment. These insights provide concrete and conceptual elements to incorporate when designing future Dance for Health programmes, particularly for this population.

articles.title: Status and the self: Socioeconomic inequality in core beliefs
articles.authors: Niklas Schulte; Matthias Ziegler; Patrick Mussel
articles.abstract: In popular discourse, voices repeatedly claim that personal success is largely a matter of mindset. In psychological science, such claims correspond to self-related core beliefs—generalized self-representations. Yet the absence of a comprehensive framework has prevented systematic study of their links to socioeconomic inequality. Building on the CorBel model—an integrative taxonomy of 97 belief nuances derived via natural language processing—we analyzed two preregistered, SES-representative national samples (Germany: N = 435, UK: N = 266). Across countries, positive beliefs (e.g., competence, autonomy, trust) were associated with higher SES, whereas negative beliefs (e.g., insecurity, unworthiness, pessimism) were linked to lower SES. These associations replicated across SES indicators (education, income, wealth) and explained up to 20% of variance in SES outcomes. This study provides the first systematic mapping of how socioeconomic inequalities are mirrored in individuals’ innermost psychological constitution, identifying beliefs as potential targets for interventions with societal and policy relevance.

articles.title: Family environmental unpredictability and adolescent physiological and psychological health: The buffering role of positive school climate
articles.authors: Qianqian Gao; Danhua Lin
articles.abstract: Using a statistical-learning approach, the present study examined whether unpredictability in abuse and neglect differentially predicted adolescents’ diurnal cortisol rhythms and depressive symptoms, and whether a positive school climate moderated these associations. A total of 211 adolescents (T1: Mage = 10.82 years, SD = 0.85; 34.6% girls) participated in a four-wave longitudinal survey spanning two years. Unpredictability was operationalized as random variation across the same repeated measurements. Results indicated that unpredictability in abuse significantly predicted flatter diurnal cortisol slopes but not depressive symptoms. Abuse unpredictability also interacted with average abuse exposure: higher unpredictability was linked to fewer depressive symptoms when average exposure was high. Neglect unpredictability showed no significant associations with either cortisol rhythms or depressive symptoms. School safety and order moderated the link between abuse unpredictability and diurnal cortisol slopes, with significant effects emerging only under low school safety and order. Similarly, school support and acceptance moderated the association between neglect unpredictability and diurnal cortisol slopes. Findings suggest that abuse unpredictability has stronger implications for adolescent health than neglect unpredictability, and that a positive school climate may serve as a protective factor for adolescents experiencing adverse family contexts.

articles.title: Asking Open-Ended Questions Promotes Personal Goal Attainment in Integrative Negotiations
articles.authors: Matteo Di Stasi; Alison Wood Brooks; Jordi Quoidbach
articles.abstract: Prior research suggests that asking more questions improves outcomes in cooperative conversations, and a vast wisdom literature espouses the power of asking questions during conflictual conversations, too: negotiation experts suggest that questions invite counterparts to disclose information and, in doing so, put askers at an informational advantage. But is this advice necessary—and is it effective? We analyzed 61,057 speech turns from transcripts of 309 dyadic integrative negotiations and used natural language processing to estimate how often people ask questions, what types of questions they ask, and how well question-asking predicts personal goal attainment (Study 1; n = 618 MBA students). Open-ended questions were rare, occurring about once every four minutes (8% of turns). Yet, asking more open-ended questions was robustly associated with personal goal attainment. Closed-ended questions and non-question statements were not reliably related to goal attainment. We then tested causality in live chat negotiations: participants who were instructed to ask open-ended questions achieved higher personal gains than those instructed to ask closed-ended questions or to only make statements (Study 2; n = 1,452 online participants), and those instructed to prepare open-ended questions before their interactions outperformed those instructed to prepare statements (Study 3; n = 372 online participants). In all studies, the benefits of open-ended questions were tied to increased information elicitation and greater value creation. Collectively, these findings offer empirical support for the widely accepted—but rarely tested—claim that negotiators (and conversationalists broadly) focus excessively on influencing (by making statements) at the expense of learning (by asking questions).

articles.title: Why Norms Collapse Irreversibly: Conformity Convexity and Campaign Reactance in a Delayed Diffusion Model on Heterogeneous Networks
articles.authors: Srajal Bajpai; Ahmed Sameer
articles.abstract: Descriptive-norm campaigns that make a behaviour and its adopters visible sometimes achieve the opposite of what they intend, pushing people away from the norm being advertised. Conformity and reactance are each well characterised in isolation, but how adoption and resistance evolve jointly, and where the boundary falls between a norm that establishes itself and one that collapses, remains unclear. We propose a delayed two-susceptibility compartmental model of norm diffusion on a heterogeneous network, coupling a convex conformity kernel with a campaign-modulated reactance incidence acting on a shared, delayed perception of prevalence. The model exhibits a backward bifurcation, i.e. an endemic norm persists below the threshold that would be needed to establish it, coexisting with the norm-free state over a band bounded below by a saddle-node, and collapses once driven past that fold, with restoration of the original conditions insufficient to recover it. The analysis attributes this irreversibility to the convexity of the conformity kernel alone, while reactance does not generate the collapse but sets where it strikes, turning the most connected classes first. A stronger campaign raises the collapse threshold and so narrows rather than widens the bistable window, bounding the optimal intensity. Wherever an explicit gain condition holds, the perception delay governs the speed of consolidation or collapse but not the state reached.

articles.title: Assessment of Intervention Effectiveness in Concurrent Multiple-Baseline Designs using Within-Series and Between-Series Counterfactual Evidence
articles.authors: Rumen Manolov; René Tanious
articles.abstract: The multiple-baseline design (MBD) is the most commonly used type of single-case experimental design (SCED) in the behavioral sciences. In the context of recent discussions regarding the usefulness and internal validity of concurrent and nonconcurrent MBDs, we suggest a data analytical and graphical approach for concurrent MBDs using counterfactuals, allowing for within- and between-series comparisons. The data analytical approach is linked to principles from the existing SCED literature: selecting a quantification of effect that represents the researchers’ expectations about the data pattern, focusing on tentative causal inference, and summarizing the results without losing sight of the variability across series (i.e., tiers). The approach is formalized as a series of four steps, highlighting counterfactuals and a proposed graphical representation. The steps and the suggested plot are illustrated in the context of real-world data and can easily be implemented using the R code developed for providing both the numerical results and graphs.

articles.title: When Single-Case Data are Ordinal (or Variable) and Exhibit Monotonic Trend
articles.authors: Rumen Manolov; Antonio Solanas
articles.abstract: There are many different data analytical procedures applicable to data obtained via single-case experimental designs, with mean differences, regression-based procedures, and nonoverlap indices being among the most frequently used ones. The possibilities are reduced when the data are ordinal and/or variable and cannot be meaningfully summarized by straight lines. For such scenarios, nonoverlap indices become prominent. The current text deals with the quantification of trend in the context of using nonoverlap indices, commenting some drawbacks of existing options and making a new proposal for assessing monotonic trend. This proposal is related to existing data analytical principles and is illustrated with several examples. The aim of the review of existing options and of the new proposal is to ignite further discussion regarding how to deal with trend without assuming that a straight line (or any specific nonlinear model) is a good representation of the data, while also taking into account the possibility that any trend may level off by reaching an upper or lower bound. A new graphical representation is proposed to accompany the quantification of monotonic trend.

articles.title: Toward a mechanistic understanding of neuromodulation in addiction: A systematic review of cognitive effects following non-invasive brain stimulation
articles.authors: Eunhwi Lee; Seungbeen Song; Woo-Young Ahn
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) techniques have emerged as promising interventions for addiction, yet their effects on the cognitive processes underlying addictive behaviors remain inconclusive.
Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we systematically reviewed sham-controlled studies identified through PubMed, PsycInfo, and EMBASE (search through November 2025) examining the effects of NIBS on cognitive processes in substance use and behavioral addictions. 39 studies were included and narratively synthesized across four cognitive domains: attentional and behavioral bias, inhibitory control, valuation and decision-making, and reward processing and learning.
Results: Across studies, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) was the predominant stimulation target, with excitatory protocols (e.g., anodal tDCS, high-frequency rTMS) most commonly applied. Effect direction analysis indicated domain-specific patterns: NIBS most consistently modulated reward-related learning processes, whereas attentional bias measures showed little evidence of change. Findings for inhibitory control and decision-making tasks were mixed.
Discussion: Results suggest that some cognitive processes may be more sensitive to cortical neuromodulation than others. A major limitation of the current literature is the reliance on aggregate task performance measures, which obscure the specific cognitive computations influenced by stimulation. Future research may benefit from applying computational modeling approaches, particularly reinforcement learning frameworks, to decompose behavioral performance into latent parameters with clear psychological interpretations. Such approaches may enable more precise mechanistic understanding of NIBS effects and support the development of targeted neuromodulation interventions for addiction.

articles.title: The Relationship between Emotional Intelligence and Emotion Regulation: A Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Hester Xiao; Kit S Double; Rebecca Pinkus; Muuskan Kalwani; Riley Leckie; Carolyn MacCann
articles.abstract: Emotional intelligence (EI) reflects individuals’ capacities, whereas emotion regulation involves the behaviours people use to manage emotions. This meta-analysis (n = 115 studies, k = 923 effects) examined associations between EI and 20 common regulation processes, considering three major EI streams and four ability branches. EI was positively associated with putatively adaptive processes (direct situation modification, positive reappraisal, deep acting, seeking help), negatively associated with putatively maladaptive processes (avoidance, denial, surface acting, catastrophizing, self-blame, expressive suppression, substance use), and positively associated with religious coping and humor. EI stream moderated effects for direct situation modification, acceptance, positive reappraisal, distraction, and seeking help (weaker for ability EI than other streams; weaker for mixed EI than self-rated EI). EI branch moderated associations of ability EI with direct situation modification and seeking help, with stronger effects for emotion management. Overall, findings indicate that emotionally intelligent individuals primarily regulate emotions by addressing problems (direct modification, seeking help) or reframing situations (positive reappraisal), reflecting a tendency to use engagement rather than disengagement regulation processes. Test format (ability vs. rating scale) and theoretical model (ability vs. mixed) significantly influenced effect sizes. This meta-analysis advances understanding of emotion regulation as a key pathway linking EI to positive outcomes.

articles.title: Man vs Machine: Electrodermal and Behavioural Responses to Human and AI‑Generated Faces
articles.authors: Giulia Panozzo
articles.abstract:
As technology advances and AI-generated faces increasingly resemble real human faces, it remains unclear whether human autonomic responses differ when viewing human and synthetic faces before explicit judgement. This study investigated whether electrodermal activity (EDA) can reveal pre-conscious physiological differences during the visual presentation of human versus AI-generated faces. Twenty-three adults (25–65 years) viewed static faces from three categories—human, hyper-realistic AI, and less realistic AI-generated faces—while continuous EDA was recorded during an initial passive viewing phase. Participants then completed an active categorisation task in which they classified each face as "human" or "AI", followed by a questionnaire assessing prior exposure to AI-generated content.
Human faces elicited significantly higher EDA than both AI-generated categories during passive viewing, indicating stronger autonomic engagement with human faces than synthetic faces prior to explicit categorisation. In the active task, participants correctly classified 89% of human faces and 99% of less realistic AI faces, but only 78% of hyper-realistic AI faces, misclassifying 22% of them as human (60/276 trials across participants). These findings suggest that autonomic sensitivity to human social stimuli persists even when highly realistic AI faces are behaviourally difficult to distinguish from human faces, indicating that pre-conscious physiological responses do not straightforwardly translate into explicit behavioural discrimination. Self-reported familiarity with AI-generated content predicted behavioural performance but was unrelated to autonomic differentiation, further supporting a dissociation between physiological and explicit measures.
Overall, the findings suggest that autonomic responses, explicit behavioural judgements, and prior experience capture complementary aspects of Human–AI face perception. Together, they indicate that increasing visual realism alone is insufficient to eliminate autonomic differentiation. These findings provide a basis for understanding how increasingly realistic AI-generated media are processed and, ultimately, for examining their broader societal implications, with relevance for the ethical development and deployment of synthetic media.

Keywords: electrodermal activity, human-AI perception, Uncanny Valley, autonomic nervous system, artificial intelligence

articles.title: A Single-Arm Longitudinal Pilot Study of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu as a Mental Health Intervention for Combat Veterans with Military-Connected Disabilities
articles.authors: Jack Ryan Kaufman; Wyatt R. Evans; Robert W. Haley; C. Munro Cullum
articles.abstract: Combat veterans experience increased incidences of depression, anxiety, and PTSD, along with challenges when adjusting to life post-discharge, but have been under-served using traditional mental health treatments. Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu has emerged as potentially therapeutic for combat veterans, although empirical support is lacking. A single-arm pre-post pilot study was used to evaluate seven psychosocial outcomes among participants from the We Defy Foundation program (n = 40; 87.5% male; Mage = 41.1, SD = 5.8). The primary outcomes measured were post-traumatic stress severity (PTSD Checklist for DSM-5; PCL-5), depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-9; PHQ-9), anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7; GAD-7), and Military-Civilian Transition Quality (M2CQ). Secondary outcomes included Self-Efficacy (General Self-Efficacy Scale; GSE), Functional Disability (World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule; WHODAS 2.0), and Life Satisfaction (Satisfaction with Life Scale; SWLS). Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), 3 months (T3; n = 34), and 6 months (T6; n = 23, final). Results revealed significant improvements in the four primary outcomes, which demonstrated high symptom severity scores at baseline, at both T3 (Cohen’s dz = .52-.63) and T6 (dz = .84-1.04) after applying the Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. Two of the three secondary outcomes achieved statistical significance at T3 (GSE and SWLS) and WHODAS became statistically significant at T6. These preliminary findings indicate BJJ participation resulted in positive accumulative mental health improvements for this veteran population and provides a promising therapeutic target for future studies.

articles.title: Stabilizing Variables in Motor Control and Learning: A Control-Theoretic Account
articles.authors: Ian S. Howard
articles.abstract:
Motor learning is shaped by history, context, and task structure. Phenomena such as washout, rebound, spontaneous recovery, savings, interference, and context-dependent generalization are often interpreted using frameworks such as state-space adaptation and contextual inference. In such accounts, the nervous system infers latent contexts or task states that help select, weight, or update distinct internal models or control policies. Here we propose a complementary control-theoretic account grounded in stabilizability. We argue that behavior and learning may depend in part on the construction, maintenance, and loss of stabilizing variables: internal dynamical states used by the controller to generate corrective action and support stable control under delay, noise, and bandwidth limitations. From this viewpoint, phenomena sometimes described in contextual-inference terms may also reflect changes in whether task-relevant variables are available in a control-feasible form.
To illustrate this principle, we used minimal plant-coupled simulations in which controller-internal compensatory states were added to feedback controllers. Appropriately matched internal variables reduced tracking error under constant-load and viscous perturbations, while retained states produced aftereffect-like behavior after perturbation removal. We also use a velocity-dependent curl-field reaching example to show how delay, noise, and contextual identifiability constrain online compensation. These examples are illustrative control demonstrations, rather than full biological models. The framework therefore offers a control-feasibility level of analysis: motor learning may depend not only on error, reward, or contextual inference, but also on whether the variables available to the controller are reliable, low-latency, identifiable, and sufficiently control-relevant to support stable behavior.

articles.title: Individual Differences in Second Language Word Learning: Toward a Neurocognitive Model of Vocabulary Learning Capacity
articles.authors: Manuela Macedonia; Lihui Hu; Brian Mathias
articles.abstract: Vocabulary acquisition in a second language (L2) is a complex, multifactorial process shaped by individual differences in cognitive, linguistic, and motivational capacities. This paper introduces the Word Learning Capacity Model (WLCM), a developmental and neurocognitively informed framework for understanding and assessing individual capacity for L2 word learning. Drawing on empirical work in cognitive neuroscience, psycholinguistics, and bilingualism, we identify eight candidate contributors to L2 word learning capacity: phonological memory, working memory, fast mapping, semantic network strength, cross-linguistic awareness, metalinguistic awareness, lexical inference, and motivation and engagement. Each contributor is linked to candidate neural correlates and supported by validated or commonly used behavioral assessments. The WLCM organizes these contributors into a framework for examining learner strengths, vulnerabilities, and developmental sources of variation. The model is intended primarily as a multidimensional research framework for testing how learner profiles predict the acquisition, retention, and use of new L2 words, and requires future psychometric validation across languages, age groups, and learner populations. The WLCM thus provides a testable structure for linking neurocognitive theory to measurement and, ultimately, to more responsive language instruction.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence as an Augmented Partner in School Consultation: Applications Across the Problem-Solving Process
articles.authors: Shengtian Wu; Cara Dillon; Adam Lockwood
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly influencing various fields. Its emergence has a strong potential to impact school consultation practice by reducing administrative burden, providing extensive support for the consultee, and supporting data-based decision-making. Although school consultants, such as school psychologists, increasingly adopt AI in summarization, writing, and recommendations during school consultation, the ethical use of AI in consultation has not yet been clearly delineated. This article describes how AI can support four phases of a well-established consultation modality, problem-solving consultation. We propose an augmented triad framework, where AI plays a partner that assists consultants with organization, reflection, skill development, follow-up intervention support, and data visualization. This framework also highlights ethical considerations when using AI in each phase. The article concludes with implications for research and practice that encourage empirical evaluation of AI use in school consultation, safeguards for privacy and bias, as well as professional training for responsible and equitable integration of AI into school consultation.

articles.title: Professional well-being among creative arts and psychomotor therapists in the Netherlands: A Job Demands-Resources perspective
articles.authors: Harm Damen; Jackie Heijman; Suzanne Haeyen
articles.abstract: Professional well-being among Creative Arts and Psychomotor Therapies (CAPTs) professionals remains understudied. This study examined compassion satisfaction, secondary traumatic stress, and burnout among CAPTs professionals in the Netherlands, and investigated how job demands and resources relate to burnout using the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 598 CAPTs professionals who completed the Professional Quality of Life Scale and the Questionnaire on Professional Well-Being of CAPTs Professionals. Results showed high compassion satisfaction (M = 39.7, SD = 4.4) and low burnout (M = 21.9, SD = 4.3) compared to most international benchmark groups, yet high levels of secondary traumatic stress (M = 20.1, SD = 4.8), with scores exceeding 70% of benchmark samples. Latent regression analyses indicated positive associations of secondary traumatic stress (B = 0.40, p < .001) and work pressure (B = 0.29, p < .001) with burnout. Compassion satisfaction (B = -0.30, p < .001) and work climate (B = -0.17, p < .01) functioned as protective resources. Work-related sickness absence (≥ 3 months) was positively associated with burnout (B = 0.20, p < .05). The interaction between work pressure and work climate was significant but small (B = 0.06, p < .05), suggesting limited buffering. These findings highlight secondary traumatic stress as a risk factor and emphasize that structural work pressure reduction is essential for preventing burnout, as resources provide only limited protection against high demands. Organizations should implement preventive measures for secondary traumatic stress and prioritize structural work pressure reduction.

articles.title: Visual confidence is an online process
articles.authors: Marshall L. Green; Dobromir Rahnev
articles.abstract: Although several prominent models of visual metacognition postulate that confidence is a post-decision process, many other models posit that confidence is an online process. To adjudicate between these two theories, we developed a novel task that requires continuous report of both choice and confidence. Participants estimated the global motion direction of dot motion stimuli by centering a confidence interval on the perceived direction and provided confidence by adjusting the width of the confidence interval. For the first half-second, participants exhibited chance performance, low confidence, and chance-level confidence-accuracy correlation. This initial period was followed by a rapid simultaneous increase in both accuracy and the confidence-accuracy correlation, suggesting that confidence did not exhibit any post-decision delay. Critically, a cross-correlogram analysis demonstrated no lag between the accuracy and confidence time-courses. These data were explained by an online model of confidence, where decision and confidence are made simultaneously. Altogether, our results strongly suggest that confidence is an online process that is computed simultaneously with the perceptual decision and challenge models where confidence is strictly a post-decision process.

articles.title: Gender gaps in autonomy persist among remote IT professionals, whereas work-family conflict varies by age: a cross-sectional survey
articles.authors: Prasantha Rayner Fernando; Crissie M. Jameson
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This study examined whether gender and age are associated with job autonomy and directional work-family conflict among remote information technology professionals.
Design/methodology/approach: A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 105 remote IT professionals. Gender differences were tested with independent-samples t-tests, and age-group differences were examined with one-way ANOVAs followed by Tukey post-hoc comparisons.
Findings: Male participants reported higher overall autonomy than female participants, with significant differences for decision-making and work methods autonomy but not scheduling autonomy. Age was associated with all autonomy dimensions. Family-to-work conflict was highest among participants aged 25–34, whereas work-to-family conflict peaked among those aged 45–54.
Research limitations/implications: The cross-sectional self-report design limits causal inference, and the oldest age group was small.
Practical implications: Remote-work equity assessments should address substantive discretion, not only schedule flexibility, and support should be tailored across career stages.
Originality/value: The study shows that demographic differences in autonomy and work-family conflict remain visible in remote IT work and extends job design and inter-role conflict research to this context.
Keywords: remote work; job autonomy; work-family conflict; IT professionals; gender; age

articles.title: Then a miracle occurs: explicating measurement theory to achieve justified validity and facilitate epistemic iteration
articles.authors: Gjalt - Jorn Peters; Rik Crutzen; Christine van Vliet; Vanessa Torres van Grinsven; Ron Jonathan Pat-El; Stefan L.K. Gruijters
articles.abstract:
At the heart of psychology’s replication crisis and underlying measurement and theory crises, the need for conceptual clarification and more rigorous measurement practices have been identified. These observations align with the persistent plea to bridge the chasm between substantive psychological theory and psychometrics and methodology. 

We introduce Narrative Response Models (NRMs) as a tool to study the validity of measurement instruments of aspects of the human psyche. In contrast to the commonly employed psychometric approaches that are based on the construct validity theory perspective, studying validity with NRMs allows claims of validity that are based on understanding of how a measurement instrument works. NRMs were designed to be easy to use but epistemologically potent, contributing to conceptual clarification.. NRMs can be developed using expert knowledge, synthesis of theory and evidence, or inductive approaches. Once developed, NRMs can guide validation efforts using cognitive interviews, response process evaluation, experiments, or computational modeling, in an iterative process comprising adaptation of an item, construct definition, and the NRM connecting both.

NRMs answer the call to again align “validity” with the common-sense definition: whether a measurement instrument measures what it was designed to measure.

articles.title: How The Bias-Variance Tradeoff Shapes Human Strategy Selection
articles.authors: Maximilian Maier; Falk Lieder; Tom Griffiths
articles.abstract: The extent to which biased decision-making is adaptive is one of the longest-debated questions in cognitive science. We investigate whether people adaptively select decision strategies following an optimal bias-variance trade-off: decision strategies that integrate (imperfect) estimates of many uncertain attributes may be unbiased but suffer from high variance, so simpler (biased) decision strategies can be more accurate when uncertainty is high. Using a new multi-attribute choice task, in which we manipulate uncertainty by varying the reliability of the estimates of different attributes across conditions, we provide an empirical demonstration that people indeed adaptively shift their decision strategies in response to environmental uncertainty: participants were more likely to use single-attribute decision-making under high uncertainty and to integrate all attributes under low uncertainty. These findings provide evidence that the bias-variance trade-off is a key principle shaping human strategy selection.

articles.title: People Missallocate Risk-Reduction Investments in Decisions Under Extinction Risk
articles.authors: Maximilian Maier; Leah Wu; Henrik Singmann
articles.abstract:
Many real-world decisions involve small probabilities of irrecoverable loss, where failure eliminates the possibility of making future decisions. Such decisions under extinction risk differ fundamentally from standard risky choice. We study how people allocate resources to reduce extinction risks. Participants play 100 trials with variable extinction probabilities of 2.5%, 5%, and 10%. If a participant draws the extinction outcome, they lose all accumulated bonus payment and are precluded from further earnings. Participants can reduce extinction risk by investing earnings: for every £0.02 invested, the extinction probability in the current trial is halved. We use dynamic programming to derive the optimal investment decision for each
choice and compare it with participants’ investments. Our results show that participants overinvest in reducing small risks, underinvest in reducing larger risks, and fail to adjust their investment appropriately across trials, leading them to go extinct at a higher rate compared to the optimal strategy.

articles.title: A Single-Arm Longitudinal Pilot Study of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu as a Mental Health Intervention for Combat Veterans with Military-Connected Disabilities
articles.authors: Jack Ryan Kaufman; Wyatt R. Evans; Robert W. Haley; C. Munro Cullum

articles.title: Parental Digital Tracking of Adolescents’ School Performance, Location, and Finances: Widespread, Often Accepted, and Linked to Overprotection
articles.authors: Savannah Boele; Anne Bülow; Loes Keijsers
articles.abstract: Introduction. Digital tracking tools are now at parents’ fingertips, raising concerns about infringement on adolescents’ autonomy, privacy, and well-being. Despite growing concerns about parental digital surveillance, empirical research beyond location tracking remains limited. This study examined parental digital tracking across three key domains: school performance, location, and finances. Methods. This is a multi-informant, cross-sectional survey study (2024) including 525 Dutch parent–adolescent dyads (adolescents: Mage=14.1, range=11-18; 53% female; parents: Mage=46.7, 81% mothers). A second sample (N = 175 dyads; 2019) tested replication and changes over time. Results. In 2024, nearly all parents (99.6%) tracked at least one domain. Most adolescents accepted tracking, though location tracking was accepted less. Younger, less educated parents, and mothers tracked more frequently, particularly school performance. Adolescents following a lower secondary educational track were tracked more frequently. Younger adolescents and boys experienced more frequent school tracking, whereas older adolescents were tracked more frequently in location. Digital tracking was unrelated to adolescent well-being (e.g., anxiety symptoms) but positively associated with parental control- and fear-related factors (e.g., overprotection, dangerous worldviews). School and location tracking increased over the past five years, as did adolescents’ acceptance of tracking. Conclusions. Parental digital tracking appears a common tool for many parents today and its frequent use may reflect parental insecurities, with no clear link to adolescent maladjustment. Longitudinal research is needed to examine whether digital tracking reassures parents or reinforces fears, which might undermine parents’ - and potentially also adolescents’ - well-being.

articles.title: The Microsystem Matters: Using machine learning to identify moderators of longitudinal  parenting effects on adolescent internalizing problems
articles.authors: Savannah Boele; Stefanos Mastrotheodoros; Caspar J. Van Lissa
articles.abstract:
Background: Despite decades of research on parenting, it remains unclear why the same 
practices benefit some adolescents but not others. Prior research on moderators that could explain 
heterogeneous parenting effects has typically examined just one or a few potential factors and 
yielded mixed findings. The present study cast a wider net, evaluating 129 potential moderators 
to identify the most important determinants of heterogeneity in within-family parenting effects on 
adolescents’ internalizing problems. Methods: Participants were 7,928 adolescents and their 
7,840 mothers and 6,777 fathers enrolled in the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children 
(LSAC). Parents reported on parenting (warmth, inductive reasoning, low angry parenting) and 
adolescents reported on internalizing problems for four biannual waves (age 10-16). Time-lagged 
within-family parenting effects were estimated using Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel 
Models, and SEM-forests were used to evaluate 129 time-invariant moderators spanning multiple 
levels of the bioecological model. Results: On average, all parenting practices negatively 
predicted internalizing problems, with substantial heterogeneity across families. The effect of 
maternal warmth was most heterogeneous, being protective in some families and harmful in 
others. The most influential moderators across all practices were family microsystem 
characteristics, in particular father involvement and parental life difficulties. Despite being an 
important moderator, father involvement’s marginal moderating effects were approximately flat, 
suggesting that it might interact with other family characteristics. Parental life difficulties 
diminished protective parenting effects. Conclusions: Macro-timescale parenting effects on 
adolescent internalizing problems are heterogeneous across families, and this heterogeneity 
depends primarily on the family microsystem rather than on individual adolescent characteristics. 
These findings suggest that one-size-fits-all approaches to parenting research and intervention are 
insufficient, and call for greater attention to the family context.

articles.title: Awareness is Predictably Lossy
articles.authors: Ariel berlinger; Ariel Goldstein; Baruch Eitam
articles.abstract: When something is plainly in view, are we always aware of seeing it, and is awareness always beneficial? We tested whether a clearly visible but task-irrelevant feature can fail to become reportable while still guiding behavior. Across four experiments (N = 584), participants viewed meaningful two-part objects under prolonged, unmasked exposure, with only one-part task-relevant. When unexpectedly asked to report the irrelevant part, participants performed at chance; yet the same feature reliably guided choices in a perceptual comparison task (55% and 60% correct; chance = 33%). The advantage belonged to the least aware: participants who reported noticing no change outperformed those who did, an inverse relationship confirmed in a large preregistered replication. Awareness is not simply stronger perception, but a selective transformation of what we see.

articles.title: Dissociating Eye and Mouth Contributions to Dynamic Face Processing with Frequency Tagging
articles.authors: Yasemin Gunindi; Çiçek Güney; Huseyin Ozkan; Nihan Alp
articles.abstract: Dynamic face perception depends on how local information from moving face parts is used within the broader configuration of the face. The present study used a temporal-direction discrimination task to examine the part-based neural contributions of the eyes and mouth during dynamic face processing. Across two experiments, Turkish and non-Turkish speakers judged whether muted videos of neutral faces articulating Turkish speech were presented forward or backward in time, while the eye and mouth regions were independently frequency-tagged in the EEG. Face orientation and blink presence were manipulated to assess how canonical face configuration and local dynamic cues shape part-based responses. Behaviorally, participants discriminated temporal direction above chance, with higher sensitivity for upright faces and with-blink face videos. Turkish speakers showed higher sensitivity than non-Turkish speakers specifically for upright faces, suggesting that language familiarity facilitated behavioral judgments when speech-related facial information was available in its canonical configuration. In the EEG, frequency-tagged responses were stronger for the mouth than for the eye, possibly reflecting the more sustained visual input generated by continuous articulatory mouth movements compared with the more transient motion in the eye region. Blink presence selectively enhanced eye-related responses, and face orientation modulated the differentiation between eye- and mouth-related responses. However, temporal direction did not produce a robust overall difference in frequency-tagged response strength, and language group did not modulate the tagged responses. Overall, the findings suggest that temporal-direction discrimination relies on how eye- and mouth-related cues are used within the face configuration, while frequency-tagged EEG responses reveal condition-dependent differences in the visual encoding of these dynamic face parts.

articles.title: Implementing Dimensional and Transdiagnostic Mental Health Assessment in Psycho-Oncology: Validation of the HiTOP Brief Report (HiTOP-BR) in Cancer Survivors
articles.authors: Jai Carmichael; Annika Hegde; Martin Sellbom; Nicolas Hart; Darren Haywood
articles.abstract: Assessment of psychopathology among cancer survivors often relies on measures of generalized psychological distress or unstructured approaches, limiting the comprehensive assessment of mental health difficulties. Contemporary dimensional and transdiagnostic frameworks, such as the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP), offer a framework for more comprehensive structure and assessment. We evaluated the psychometric properties of the 45-item HiTOP Brief Report (HiTOP-BR) in cancer survivors. Participants were 728 adults with a current (n = 155) or past (n = 573) cancer diagnosis who were recruited and completed the HiTOP-BR online alongside other cancer-specific measures. All primary and secondary scales demonstrated good internal consistency (αs and ωs > .80). Relative to general community data, participants with current cancer showed elevations across the Somatoform, Internalizing, Thought Disorder, Antagonism, and p-Factor dimensions and scored higher than participants with past cancer across all dimensions except Detachment. Among participants with past cancer, elevations relative to general community data were confined to the Somatoform spectrum. Confirmatory factor analysis broadly supported the proposed six-spectra structure, with all items loading meaningfully on their intended factors. A bifactor model identified a strong general psychopathology factor (ωH = .84), although substantial variance remained attributable to the specific spectra (ECV = .56). Higher HiTOP-BR scores were associated with poorer physical functioning and greater fear of cancer progression and recurrence. The HiTOP-BR appears to be a reliable and valid tool for assessing psychopathology dimensions that may be elevated among cancer survivors and facilitating implementation of dimensional and transdiagnostic approaches within psycho-oncology.
